The House proceeded to consider the amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 36, respecting Banks and Banking.
What are these amendments?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. T. WHITE (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amendments made by the
Senate are of a comparatively minor character. In section 15, the application presented for certificate to the Treasury Board

must be a sworn statement. In sub-section 8 of section 16, the word 'hereinbefore' is substituted for the word 'heretofore.'
In section 43 a provision was made whereby it was compulsory for the bank to open and maintain in each province in which it has resident shareholders, a shares registry office, in order that shares belonging to such residents might be transferred there. That was inserted not by reason of any request of shareholders or of banks, but having regard to the fact that under the present Bank Act it is possible that more than one province c.an collect succession duties upon the shares of shareholders - of chartered banks. That results from a decision of Chancellor Boyd in Ontario, who held that a bank's shares are domiciled in the province in which the bank has its head office. Therefore it is possible for the Government of Ontario and the Government of Quebec each to collect succession duties in respect of shares belonging to the estate of a deceased shareholder resident in the province of Quebec. In the committee, it- was thought that, if a provision were inserted in the Act whereby shares might be completely transferred in any province, although the head office of the bank did not happen to be in that province, it might possibly have the effect that only the province in which the deceased was domiciled would be able to collect succession duties in respect of his shares. In other words, it would make the shares follow the domicile of the owner, and I believe that is the general law in respect of personal property. It was doubtful whether the amendment inserted by the committee and approved by this House would effectuate that purpose. The opinion of the deputy Minister of Justice was obtained, but was not very positive in its character. He indicated that if this amendment were inserted, and if action were brought, the courts would probably give effect to the Dominion legislation because the banks come under Dominion jurisdiction. The banks pointed out that this would entail considerable inconvenience to them and some inconvenience to the shareholders. They further pointed out that the transfer of bank shares was a very important matter; that every care had to be taken against fraud or negligence, and that the head office organization in connection with the transfer of shares was very complete and efficient. They also pointed out that they would have to establish a similar organization in each of the provinces, and that this would be no convenience to shareholders because shares are sold principally in Montreal or Toronto. The Senate, instead of allowing the amendment to stand, making it compulsory for the banks to establish these offices, made it permissive, contending that the section, permissive as it now is, is quite as effectual as if it were mandatory.
That is to say, if the shares may be completely transferred in a province, the courts would hold that the domicile of the shares is with the owner resident in the province, in other words, if the banks ' may ' open offices at which shares may be completely and effectually transferred, the same legal consequences, in so far as the domicile of the shares is concerned, will follow as if the section were mandatory. I am of the view, especially as the Senate appears to have given the matter careful consideration, that we should concur in the amendment.
In sub-section 4 of section 54, the word ' detailed ' is struck out before the words ' profit and loss account.' This amendment was introduced in the committee by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy). The banks are in the habit of presenting to the shareholders simply a statement showing net profits after deducting amounts written off for bad and doubtful debts, cost of administration, &c. It was thought it would be in the interest of the shareholders that that statement should be elaborated a little. It has been pointed out, however, that the word ' detailed ' in itself is equivocal and ambiguous, and that the sub-section does not particularize or indicate by any form, as a schedule to the Act, the extent of the detailed information to be given. As the sub-section stood, a bank could put its own interpretation upon the word, and the Senate practically unanimously came to the conclusion that it should be struck out. As i.t appears to be rather of minor importance, I think that we should concur in this change also.
The next amendment is in section 56. In the interpretation clause of the Act the words ' members of the association ' mean the general managers of the banks. Under the Act incorporating the Canadian Bankers' Association, the words ' members of the association ' mean more than this, and tho Senate has struck out in the interpretation clause the words ' and members of the association means the general managers of the banks '; and in section 56 they have struck out the -words ' the members of the association,' and have inserted the words ' the general managers of the banks,' and then in parenthesis: ' or, in the absence of the general manager of any bank, the official designated by him; or, in default of such designation, the principal officer of the bank next in authority.' Therefore the section as amended by the Senate reads:
The general managers of the banks (or, in the absence of the general manager of any bank, the official designated by him; or, in default of such designation, the principal officer of the bank next in authority) shall, at a meeting duly called for the purpose.
Appoint the auditors. In other words, this follows the wording in the Act incorporating the Canadian Bankers' Associa-

tion, and is to provide for action on the part of the general manager, or,' in his absence, by some one delegated in his place. It does not interfere with the principle that the general managers of the several banks shall name the auditors.
The next amendment is in connection with seetion 72. The Bill as it left the House provided:
The Treasury Board shall make regulations providing for the disinfection and sterilization by the several hanks of all hank notes and Dominion notes which have come into the bank's possession before a re-issue thereof to the public.	.
This is a matter that was discussed at some length in the Banking and Commerce Committee, and we reached the conclusion that it would be well to make it compulsory for the banks to sterilize their own notes and Dominion notes that come into their possession, this to be done in the interest of public health. Since the Bill left the House there has been a report by a public officer in the United States, whose name I do not recall at the moment, to the effect that germs are not found upon bank notes, although the bank notes may be soiled and old. While I do not regard that as conclusive by any means, and while I think it is quite probable that filthy bank notes carry the proportion of germs we should naturally expect, at the same time, before the Treasury Board makes these regulations we desire to have time to inquire into the subject, and to have bacteriological tests made. The United States official to whom I have referred, evidently reached the conclusion that the ink on the bank bills did not afford a congenial lodging place for germs, and that therefore it was unnecessary to have bank bills disinfected. It is my intention to have the matter investigated carefully and bacteriological tests made, and ii it is found that soiled bank bills carry germs of kinds dangerous to the public, we can pass the regulations provided for. The Senate took that view, and substituted the word ' may ' for ' shall,' making the section permissive instead of compulsory.
In section 106 there is a verbal change due to a printer's error, changing ' there 1 into ' three.'
The next change of any importance is in section 114. It is a new amendment proposed by the Senate, and it seems to me to be unobjectionable and possibly desirable. It makes it incumbent upon the banks to transmit by registered post to the person to whom any dividend amount or balance is payable, a notice stating that such amount remains unpaid. I think those are all the changes and modifications made by the Senate. In view of the fact that they are few in number and of minor importance, that the Senate evidently gave the sections that were changed careful consideration, and that none of the principles incorporated in the Act and deemed essential by the Banking and Commerce Committee and by this House have been interfered with, I move that the amendments made by the Senate to this Bill be concurred in.

There is only one of the amendments which I would be disposed to question, but inasmuch as we are now approaching the end of the session, I do not intend to oppose the motion for concurrence in the amendments made by the Senate to this Bill. I have reference to section 43. I merely wish to say

I have listened with considerable interest to the explanation of the amendments made by the Senate as outlined by the Minister of Finance, and, if I correctly understood his position, it is this:	The adoption of these
amendments in their entirety without criticism, although they practically overrule, in a great many instances at least, the result of the efforts of the Banking and Commerce Committee during the many hours that we listened to evidence and the debate on this subject when the Bill was under consideration, it is my intention to direct the attention of the House to what may be considered by the minister to be very trifling changes. The first is with regard to the sterilization of bank bills. That was adopted by the medical men of the committee for some two or three days and some evidence was given in regard to the matter. The unanimous opinion at the end of the discussion seemed to be that it was a very desirable principle, and had been successfully followed in the United States. We are told that the amendment as suggested by the Senate is based on scientific grounds, and if I might in epigrammatic language characterize the reason for this, it is that bank -bills are obnoxious to microbes. There is no reason given to support the assumption that the bills are not unsanitary. The medical men in the Banking and Commerce Committee told us that these bills were unsafe, and that they should be sterilized, but the Senate has changed this, and there is no defence put up by the Minister of Finance for the reasons or conclusions of the Banking and Commerce Committee. In respect to another clause to which an amendment was made by the Senate, permissive power is given to the banks to establish transfer offices within the various provinces. The Banking and Commerce Committee of this House decided that the establishment of these transfer offices should be compulsory, and underlying their amendment to the original Aot was the principle that dual taxation by way of succession duties was unfair. The best evidence was given with regard to this subject, and the best legal opinion obtainable was laid before the committee. This House may not be aware that at the present time, on the decease of a person practically two taxes are in many cases levied by way of succession duties. The law of the provinces lays it down that where personal property is situated within the Tvrovincp. it. shall he taxable bv way of Mr. MACLEAN (Halifax).
succession duties, and the legislatures of some of the provinces have laid down also the principle that where the head office of a bank is in a province within which the testator or deceased did not live, a second tax will be levied. Let me cite a concrete instance. If a man dies in the province of Ontario leaving an estate sufficiently valuable to make succession duty payable, the province of Ontario levies a tax, and if the man has bank stock in the province of Quebec, the province of Quebec says that because the head office of the bank is in that province, no transfer of that stock shall take place unless a succession duty is paid to the province of Quebec. I have known cases-and I have no doubt that every lawyer from Ontario and lawyers in other provinces have had the same experience-where two duties have been paid on large estates, one to the province in which the testator lived and the other to the province in which the main office of the company was situated. The Senate get over the matter so easily, it looks so unsophisticated; they simply change the word ' shall ' to ' may,' they say that a transfer office ' may ' be established in each province. The Banking Committee laid down a principle that there should be only one tax on an estate and that that should be levied in the province in which the testator lived, on the wen known principle of law that personal property has its situ where the person owning it is domiciled. That has been set aside by the Senate, and I was surprised that the Minister of Finance did not come to the rescue of his committee because I thought he was in favour of the principle they had laid down.
Mr. WHITE (Minister of Finance).: Was the hon. gentleman present in the House when I dealt with the matter to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I mentioned what I believed to be the legal opinion of members of the Senate that in so far as the section in the form in which it left this House would accomplish what my hon. friend has in view, namely, that two provinces should not be able to collect succession duties on bank stock, the amendment would be just as effectual. In other words, if the bank may establish offices in the several provinces so that a share may be completely transferred, the legal argument is that if the court would give effect to the section with the word ' shall ' they would give precisely the same effect to the section with the word ' may.'

That is true as far as it goes, but the fallacy lies here, that if the word ' shall ' is left in the Bill, as the

Banking and Commerce Committee of this House left it, then the bank must establish these offices and all ambiguity is cleared away; but as the Senate nas amended the Bill, the banks may establish these offices if they so desire and if they do not there is no possibility of redress. In other words, the right to establish a transfer office is left with the bank and if the bank does not act there will never be a possibility of a testator getting rid of this second succession duty because I have my doubts as to whether the banks will ever act. The Banking Committee ol this House laid down the principle that banks should have transfer offices in each province because it was radically unfair that an estate should be taxed twice m regard to succession.
There is a still more radical amendment. Hour after hour, in the Banking Committee, we fought for the class of statement that should be submitted by the banks and after a great deal of discussion, following the argument of the hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy), the word ' detailed ' was put in the section. The Senate have struck that word out, and in doing so they have cut the very heart out of the section. It does not mean anything like what this House intended. The committee on Banking and Commerce, or certain sections of it, fought the interests that wanted to leave the Banking Bill exactly as it was. We fought the matter fairly, day after day, before the committee, we brought evidence to substantiate our position, and, after hours of work, we made our report. Now we find everything nullified by the stand-patters in the Senate. It is all very well to say that the Senate have killed the Navy Bill, and in so doing have thwarted the will of the people. They may have thwarted the will of the people in killing the Navy Bill, but they have equally thwarted the progressive spirit of the province of Ontario in the amendment they have made to this Bill and I sincerely trust that the House will not concur in the amendment.

I desire to associate myself with every word that has been said by the horn, member for Kingston(Mr. Nickle). I do not propose to go over in detai what he has already said, but I do say that every amendment that was forced upon an unwilling committee-I was not present a great deal of the time, and I very much regret that I was absent from th,e sittings-has been nullified and 'destroyed by the Senate, and the vital question is whether or not a few capitalists shall control the action of this Parliament. That is a large question, and I think that when we made imperative certain things that we felt should be made imperative, it was not open to the Senate of Canada to make those things
permissive, because In making them imperative, we did that which we believed to be in the best interests of the people of Canada. It is a nice thing and parliamentary institutions have come to a nice condition when, merely to gratify the caprice of the Senate, that which we said should be imperative is changed and made permissive and then we are told, forsooth, that the courts will construe the word 'may* as 'shall.' Why not leave the wording as we had it and make certain that what we wanted to secure will be secured and not depend on a lawsuit to ascertain what we mean? In the ultimate analysis, I say it will be found that the Bank Act of 1913 is the Bank Act of twenty years ago without any change, without one single step forward or one motion towards progress and reform, except in so far as audit is concerned, and the clamour of public opinion necessitated that, and in one or two small instances. This Parlia-is now in the eighth month of its session and I can say, without any fear of succes-ful contradiction, that the Bank Act over which it has laboured for six or seven months is, substantially speaking, broadly and generally, the Bank Act which was on the statute-books of Canada twenty years ago, or at least fifteen years ago, and I say that is not in accordance with the spirit of our institutions. I desire to associate myself with everything that has been said by the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle).

I am a member of the Banking Committee and I also wish to join in protest against the action of the Senate. It seems "to me strange that, after the careful inquiry made by the committee, at great length, a certain number of gentlemen should offhand, nullify the whole proceedings and make permissive what would otherwise be compulsory. They dare not fly in the face of public opinion, but are trying to effect their purpose by means of the back door.

I
think the hon. gentleman who have been expending so much indignation on this question are getting unnecessarily excited. To hear the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett) talk, one would have thought that the Banking and Commerce Committee of this House were absolutely unanimous on this and every other point. There was grave doubt as to the feasibility and advantage of the proposal to establish these offices in the way proposed here, and why there should be any tirade against the other part of this Parliament, because a collection of business men who heard the arguments in regard to this question, who considered it and all the suggestions that were made, and came to the conclusion embodied in this amendment, seems to me entirely inexplicable.

For myself, as a member of the Banking Committee, who attended the sessions of that committee, I want to protest against hon. members using the language they have used.
What about the change cutting out the word ' detailed.' That is a question on which I thought our committee was- unanimous.

I do not propose to discuss the various amendments of the Senate. The hon. member for Queens and Shelburne (Mr. McCurdy) proposed many amendments in the Banking and Commerce Committee which, had they been adopted, would have resulted in a very curious Banking Act, I only rose to' protest against this unnecessary display of indignation, which is wholly unwarranted.

I did not attend as frequently as I might have done the meetings of the Banking and Commerce Committee. One disadvantage of having our attention concentrated so much on foreign affairs is that we are not able to give a sufficient amount of attention to home affairs. deal of attention to what the minister responsible for this Act says, especially a minister who has given a lifetime to the study of this banking question. Mr. Speaker, it has been a matter of regret to me that throughout the consideration of the Bank Act in committee I was not able, by reason of some other special duties, to give the detailed attention to it that I would like to have done. I may say for the information of hon. gentlemen who smile, and especially the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Clark), that I was fortunately able to give sufficient consideration to it to be in a position to stand on my feet in Parliament and give my opinion, with the sanction of my own intelligence, and not rest it on that of any other, be he however elevated in position in this House. My opinion is that the Senate, in so far as they have ventured to interfere with this Bill, have succeeded in a large degree in emasculating from it such amendments as the more progressive element in the banking and commerce committee succeeded in making to it. My purpose in rising is to

protest that the lobbyist has secured too easy an access to the House of Commons in recent years. While it is difficult to draw the line, while it is difficult to say that the lobbyist shall come this far and no farther, that he shall proceed to this door and not within it, it is not difficult to arrive at the conclusion that the lobbyist has too easy access both to this and the other House and that he interferes far beyond the limits within which he should be confined. I am informed that within the other House, while this Bill was under consideration, the paid solicitor of the Bankers Association sat within the rail of that House, or at all events immediately without it, and that he went so far as to interfere with statements being made by Senators on the floor of the House. That being the case, it would be a matter of extreme surprise to me if this Bill had come back unemasculated. We should address ourselves to the question and decide once ' and for all what shall be the rights of lobbyists, and what shall be the rights of representatives of interests in these corridors, in committees and in this House generally. If we decide that we will do a lot to remove the distrust that exists, and has existed for many years among the people of Canada, a distrust that, I venture to say, is not altogther unfounded.

I have paid some attention to the amendments made by the Senate to the Bank Act. That with reference to disinfection leaves it to the minister's department to say whether the requirement in that regard shall be followed or not. I think we can agree that it is in very safe hands and if the minister finds upon investigation that disinfection is necessary there is no doubt that it will be done. As to the word ' detail,' I agree with my hon. friend from Bed Deer (Mr. Clark) that the minister in charge of the department is very capable and I believe that if he finds it necessary to improve the character of the returns made by the banks, steps will be taken for that purpose. This is not like the laws of the Medes and Persians; we can insist upon the returns being more elaborate if necessary next year. I think that the amendment which they have made to the penalty clause improves it as compared with the form in which we sent it to the Senate. I understand from the minister that this amendment was largely suggested by his own department and I know that Mr. Boss of the Finance Department has a good deal of knowledge upon this subject. With reference to what the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) has said with regard to lobbying, I would say that I have been here for three or four years and no man has ever approached me to lobby me in the general sense of the term. I have never been asked
to support a Bill previous to its going to the committee. I do not know why, but I have always been given a wide berth since I have sat upon any of the committees of this House. Since I have been in this House, I have taken a more or less active part on two committees.
I want to tell my hon. friend that my brother does not have to stoop to be a lobbyist for the Bankers' Association, or for any other body in this country. My brother is quite independent of any corporation in this country; he came here as a lawyer representing the Bankers' Association, and if he were asked by the leader of the Senate to take a seat on the floor of the Senate, he would have been rude to have refused. He did not come here to lobby. I venture to say there is not a man in this House who can get up and say my brother did try to lobby, and if- there is any man who can say so I would like to see him get on his feet and say so now. My brother never had anything to do with lobbying, in the sense of lobbying as generally construed by members of this House. There Is no one who resents lobbying more than I do; I refer to taking a member by the sleeve and leading him off and talking him into something that his own judgment would not let him do. But I have no necessity for defending myself here, because I am known to most of the members who attend these committees. As to my brother, the remarks of the hon. member are totally and absolutely uncalled for, and I resent them.

May I be permitted as a matter of privilege to say that the only reference I made at all to the gentleman referred to by the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was as to what took place in the Senate. I said that was my information. If the hon. gentleman is in a position to rise in his place and deny the correctness of that statement, then he will say somee thing that has reference to my remarks about his brother. His remarks so far have had no reference whatever to what I said about him.

For once, at any rate, I agree measurably with the hon. member for Calgary (Mr. Bennett), in that, so far as my judgment goes, the Bank Bill as it is now before the House, is practically the Bank Act of twenty years ago. But, I want to disagree with him in the suggestion that it is as it is because of the action ot the Senate. I want to say that it is as it is because of the action of this House of Commons, and no member of this House can justify himself for the present position of that Act by raising an issue against the Senate for the trifling amendments which they have made, and which the Minister of

Finance has asked the House to agree to. My hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen), in his pathetic appeal to be protected from lobbyists, by law, or by authority of the House, or by authority of the Speaker, will certainly give out to the country an impression with regard to this House of Commons that I believe never prevailed before. I presume my hon. friend made his appeal for himself and on his own behalf, or on behalf of those who are nearly associated with him; but I want to say that so far as I am concerned, just as the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) has said, I do not require the protection of a statute to keep my skirts clear from the control of the lobbyists. I would like to know by what authority my hon. friend passes out to the public of this country such an insult upon this House of Commons, in which he sits and in which he has sat for a number of years.' My hon. friend will not protect himself from the censure of his constituents or the other people of western Canada by the excuse that he did not attend to his duties in the Banking and Commerce Committee or in tnis House, because he was otherwise engaged or because he was not able to protect himself against the lobbyists.
He was making up the closure rules.

Certainly. Nor, will he protect himself by the assertion that other members were improperly subject to the influence of lobbyists. There were a number of gentlemen, members of this House, with whom I did not agree, because I did not think their action was in accord with the best interests of the country, but I said so on the floor of Parliament, and took the responsibility of what I had to say. I would suggest respectfully to my hon. friend that before he hands out such insinuations and insults to Parliament, he should take measures to protect himself by stating his position upon the floor of Parliament.
This Bank Act is an important one; it is one that certainly brings members of Parliament personally within the danger of the great financial institutions of the country. A member of the House is taking some chances in taking a position that is in any way antagonistic to the views of these organizations. It is not for me to say that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie or any of his friends are influenced by such an idea as that; I would be sorry to think they were. But I certainly object most strenuously to the suggestion he has made, in his own protection. When he finds it necessary in order to protect himself, to insult the whole House of Commons, I think the hon. gentleman goes too far.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. B. McCURDY (Shelburne and Queens):
speechtext:
I wish to refer to the amendment made by the Senate to section 54, by which the word ' detailed ' is struck out. The hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) refers to it as a 'trifling' change. If he will give the matter a little more attention, I am sure that he will come to

the conclusion that his words were spoken without proper consideration.
That was the general impression I gathered from the tenor of the remarks of the hon. Minister of Finance. I did not refer to a particular section; I spoke of the amendments as a whole.

The hon. member I
understand, attended the Banking and Commerce Committee fairly regularly.
I was never able to attend that Committee. I dealt with the Bill in the House, not in that Committee.

Anyone who was present at this committee's sittings heard the complaints received through different channels to the effect that rates charged by banks were not at all satisfactory. Any criticism of these rates was met by tabulated statements brought forward by leading bankers, showing that the earnings of the banks did not justify a smaller 'spread' between the present 3 per cent paid on deposits and the rates, charged for discount. All their figures were based on the assumption that the profit and loss statement issued by each bank at the end of the year was correct and showed the exact earnings of the bank. Some members of the committee thought these figures did not represent the earning capacity of money used by the banks. It is well known that the figures shown as profit in the statements published annually by the banks are arrived at after deducting not only expenses of management, losses on branches which are unproductive, operating expenses of all kinds and the writing off of bad debts, but a provision for undisclosed losses still sleeping in current loans, so that, without a detailed statement of profit and loss to guide us, it is utterly impossible for an intelligent opinion to be reached as to the rate of interest earned by banks on the money which they handle. Therefore any amendment which tends to disclose the amount of money actually earned by the banks is fundamental and important. Therefore the ' slight ' amendment referred to by my hon. friend from Edmonton turns out to be a very important one.
The bankers before the Banking and Commerce committee pointed out that, if detailed statements of profit and loss were required, a tendency might ensue on the part of some banks to provide insufficient amounts out of earnings to meet losses which must occur and which are at present undisclosed. Therefore it might tend to weaken the position of such banks. This is a matter of great importance, bflt there is another very important matter for us to consider, and that is the interest of the public in the cost to them of banking facilities.
It was in order to ascertain whether or not a lower rate of interest could be charged to borrowers, or a more attractive rate of interest granted to depositors, that I thought it was necessary to have a detailed statement of profit and loss. If the real earnings of the banks, as would be shown in a * detailed ' statement are greater than those shown by the statement of earnings as the banks have published it heretofore, their argument regarding the small value to them of the money they have on deposit, etc., falls to the ground.
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) dubbed as ' curious ' a number of propositions which were made in the Banking and Commerce committee, many of which were not accepted. Of the many amendments suggested, some no doubt were inadvisable, but a great number of them had to do with different phases of the Bank Act which are at present agitating the	public mind.
I may be pardoned, perhaps, for stating that one 'curious' thing that impressed me m the committee was that nearly all the amendments of a far-reaching nature which were negatived in the Banking and Commerce committee, were negatived by the votes of members of the committee who were present in time to vote, but who had not been sufficiently 'curious' to be present at the discussions.	And, notwithstanding all the discussions and the putting forward of 'curious amendments,' as the hon0 member for Pictou calls them, not one fundamental change was made in the committee, if we except section 54 which has now been amended again by the Senate.
I am satisfied that it is possible to improve several of the important provisions of the Bank Act. Along with the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), I went to the Banking and Commerce Committee with hopes-not that radical changes would be made in our banking system, but that changes would be embodied in this measure which would facilitate business and yet make no great disturbance in the operation of the structure known as the Canadian banking system.
But I think the difficulty of dealing with this matter in committee has been impressed upon the members who have taken an active part in the committee's labours. I have about come to the conclusion that the best way to have the work done is by a reference to a small commission which will be more compact, and which, I hope, could achieve some tangible results which will work out, not only to the advantage of the public, but also to the improvement of the system and therefore to the advantage of the banks themselves.
I think that business conditions today are not such as to render violent changes desirable. Especially under



such conditions, it is not well to make sudden changes in our system. Business accustoms itself to whatever conditions surround it. We have been doing business under a certain system for a long time, and the present is not, perhaps, the time for violent change. But it _ seems to me that investigation and discussion should go on with a view to bringing about the changes that are desirable.
It is with reluctance that I feel that I must express my opinions as to the acts of a House of equal jurisdiction to this; but perhaps I may be pardoned for saying that it is my opinion that the changes proposed in the Senate are not such as are desired by the public. The changes proposed in the Banking and Commerce Committee, I am satisfied, were approved by the public. With regard particularly to section 54, I am satisfied the public are desirous of knowing what toll they pay the banking system for carrying on the banking business of the country. In taking ' out this word 'detailed' in section 54, the Senate have, in my opinion, placed themselves entirely in opposition to the public will in this matter, as they already have in other matters.

1 accept whatever responsibility rests' upon me for the Bill as it is now going through the House. I took part in the early discussion of the measure and tried to bring before the House what I considered to be a substantial issue in connection with this measure. I stated that we had an old-fashioned system, that there was an absolute need of banking currency sufficient to carry on the business of the country, and that' we ought to consider soon some means of relief. I suggested, in the first speech I	madeand I endorse what my hon, friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. McCurdy) says that there will be no solution of the bank question until we have a commission of competent men to inquire into the matter, to study it and bring in a report on which legislation can be founded. There is nothing now before the people that will cause such disappointment as the form in which this Bill is passed. There is no progress shown in this measure. We ought to have a Bank Act embodying some of the progressive ideas in banking that obtain in Europe and Australia, if not in America. After the United States Congress has dealt with this banking question-and I understand they are about to take it up -I believe this country will be more and more impressed with the idea that a commission should be appointed to study and report on. this question with a view to having another Bank Act for Canada and another Currency Act as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: with regard to such an Act as the Bank -Act is to confine a measure of progrepive-ness with caution because, even although [DOT]we may be very sure in our own minds as to the effect of a certain measure or an amendment to an existing measure, when you are dealing with a matter as complex and as far-reaching as banking, and a matter in reference to which it is so dimcult to estimate in advance all the consequences of legislative action, for my part I adhere to the view that we should proceed as I have said, progressively but cautiously, and that has been the spirit with which I approached the revision of the Act. 1 wish to pay this tribute to the Banking Committee of this House. I do not believe that any committee in any legislative assembly in Canada ever exhibited a greater interest in the subject with which_ it had to deal than div1 this committee in dealing with the Bank Act. I think everyone was impressed with the intelligence and interest with which the several sections were discussed and with the devotion to their public duty shown by all members of the committee. Personally I never sought to influence the judgment of one member with regard to any clause. The discussion was open and fair, everyone had an opportunity *of bringing forward any amendments, and having them discussed on their merits and I cheerfully bear tribute to the interest, intelligence and zeal with which the members of the committee, without exception so far as I know, devoted themselves to the very responsible duties which evolved upon them in the consideration of the Bill as it left this House. The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) has stated that there is a lack of currency in Canada at the present time. I would like to say that that lack of currency is not confined to Canada, that condition which he draws to our attention is world-wide. There is a lack of currency all over, tight money conditions prevail in Great Britain, in Germany, in France, all over the continent and in the United States. It is a worldwide condition of financial stringency, and I may say further that lack of currency has been a very general fact since the beginning of time.	[DOT]
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would not be too much to say that lack of currency is coeval and coextensive with mankind, and I think it will always be. It will always be difficult to get money, and speaking personally I think it is a good thing because if you get too much money, if you can get money by a credit system too easily, the tendency 'is to over-expend and you bring about a condition that is not desirable. The history of finance abounds with examples of what I am stating to the House. The revision of the Bank Act itself is of a very complex Mr. WHITE (Leeds).
nature and great and grave care and consideration must be devoted to^ it. So far as my attitude goes I have given to the new Act my most careful attention for a period of two years.. I have welcomed the advice of all who tendered it and sought that of those who I thought could assist me in framing a measure that would reflect credit upon the Parliament of Canada, and I think that on the whole, although I know there is a difference of opinion with regard to it, the Act we have put through is satisfactory. It is an Act, not only of the Government but of the House as a whole, because I never regarded it as a controversial measure, and attempted to deal with all of its sections with the utmost impartiality, as I think hon. members will testify. Thus the Act as it now stands substantially represents the views if not of all, at least of a very considerable majority of the members of the House.
During the year 1912-13 there has been a very great financial stringency. I do not think we have all realized just how stringent the conditions have been. In Canada I think we are not suffering more than in other countries, in fact I am greatly gratified that in Canada we have borne the strain so well. Personally I am of the view that the tight money period will gradually disappear and that in the natural course of things easy money conditions will reassert themselves. I should not be surprised if that would come more rapidly than is generally thought. In a year of this kind to revise the Bank Act has not been the easiest matter imaginable, and, under the circumstances, I feel that in moving this concurrence of the House in the amendments of the Senate for the' reasons I have given, I should express to all the members on both sides my thanks for the great assistance they have given in bringing this legislation to its present condition. It is not bv any means a perfect lot there never will be anything perfect in this world, but I believe we have made substantial progress in it and I believe that that is the view of this House.

On section 4-dangerous weapons:

What is the
nature of the amendment proposed by this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As the law stands at
present, everyone, with the exception of police officers and that class of persons, is prohibited from carrying any pistol or air gun upon his person unless he has a certificate of exemption. The first change we make is to extend that prohibition to the carrying of pistols, sheath-knives, bowie knives, daggers, stilettos, metal knuckles, skull crackers, or other offensive weapons that may be concealed upon the person, or any air gun or any device or contrivance for muffling or stopping the sound of the report of any firearm. The prohibition as it stands at present applies to the carrying of the articles referred to without having a certificate of exemption from the operation of the section. The amendment says:
' Without having a permit granted under this section.' It seemed to -be more simple to require a permit than to make a law and provide for exemption. The next change is with regard to the authority who may issue what we now call the permit, and which under the old Act was called a certificate of exemption. Under the old Act, any justice of the peace might issue a certificate of exemption. In view of the necessity of restricting the carrying of weapons of this kind, the importance of which, I regret to say, is more and more impressed upon us every day by the number of the crimes of violence committed by the use of such weapons, it has been thought well not to leave this power of issuing permits in the hands of all justices of the peace, but to restrict it to specific officers. The officers who are authorized to issue these permits under the regulations we propose are:
Any officer of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police or commissioner Dominion police or superintendent of provincial police or stipendiary or district magistrate or chief constable of any city, incorporated town or district municipality.
It has been pointed out that there are certain portions of the country where officers coming within this express legislation are not to be found, and that we should make provision for them. For the purpose of pro-

viding for such cases, I move that subsection 2 of section 4 of this Bill be amended by inserting in the fourth line thereof, after the word ' magistrate/ the words ' or sheriff.'

On section 8-seduction by employer:

It has been suggested to me by a county Crown attorney and other officers of the law that this section is going a little too far. I do not know that there has been any public demand for extending it to other classes, such as domestic servants. I did think that the section as it was had gone pretty far in that we had placed factory girls under its protection. You can understand that when a man seduces a girl employed under him in a factory he takes her away for that special purpose, but it is different in the case of a domestic servant. It opens the way very largely for blackmail. You get a girl of bad repute in your. house, the family may be away, the man may be the most innocent man in the world, she can run out of doors, raise a row, the man does not want to go before the magistrate, and he would rather settle than have his name put before the public in that way. I think this is going a little farther than the law should go. I am saying this not on my own motion, but at the suggestion of gentlemen of the Bar and others who have spoken to me about it. I think it should not be extended to domestic servants.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There has been a very persistent demand, coming from many people-
Sir WILFRID LAURIER. From whom?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
From numbers of people who have actively interested themselves in looking after domestic servants and others, especially immigrant girls coming into the country. It is not an offence if the girl be of bad repute, nor is it an offence if the girl be over twenty-one years of age. The law as it at present stands makes it an offence for an employer to seduce or have carnal connection with a girl in his employ in a factory, mill, workshop or store. The modification is simply
to strike out these words and to make it an offence for a man to seduce or have illicit carnal connection with a girl under twenty-one years of age of previous chaste repute who is in his employ. It would seem to me that such a man is a proper subject to be dealt with by the criminal law, and that if a man is guilty of an offence under the circumstances mentioned we should make provision for his punishment. It has been suggested as an objection to this provision that there is the possibility of an abuse of it. If we were to look merely at the possibility of abuse, it seems to me that it is just as possible for the factory girl, or the typewriter girl, or the girl employed in any of these places, to bring an unfounded complaint against her employer under the present law as it would be for the servant girl. If you come to a well-founded case it does seem to me that a man who so abuses the position that a girl occupies as a domestic in his own household, so to speak, a member of his own family, as to lead her astray is perhaps more blameworthy than the man who has mere casual relations with a girl in his employment in the workshop or mill. If the law be justified, and I believe it is, it would seem to me proper to extend it in this way and as against any possible abuse it might give rise to, such as blackmail or any disadvantage that might result from it in that way, we can safely consider that the protection thrown around that class of young women who have to obtain their livelihood by becoming domestic servants, is more than a balancing advantage.

I wish to throw around these young girls every protection that possibly can be given them. You have provided in section 221 for the protection of all girls under sixteen years of age. Section 213 is applicable to girls under twenty-one years of age working in shops. My hon. friend says that there is the same possibility of blackmail in regard to girls who work in shops as in regard to domestic servants. I say 4 no ' because, in the case of girls who work in shops, the circumstances surrounding the whole situation would be such that it would be more difficult to make proof against the person charged. I should think that section 211 provides ample security, and that this new provision is not necessary. My hon. friend spoke of immigrants coming out here. I have in my mind the case of a man who was charged by a girl who had come out here and who was tried in Welland county. I defended him. He was absolutely innocent and was shown to be by the evidence. It was blackmail from the beginning. He was honourably acquitted by the jury, but it was only after

a trial and an exposure which he did not like. I think it would be better to leave this section out.

I agree with the minister that a man who has a domestic servant in his employment is more blameworthy than the employer in a shop or store. But he must remember that it is often difficult to prove the previously unchaste character of the girl. The presumption is in her favour and the burden of proof is shifted to the accused. I do not think we should open the door to any blackmail. I agree with the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) that if we gave more protection in a case of that kind it might open the door to blackmail.
On section 14-neglect to provide for wife and children:
It would seem that under this section the penalty of $500 is fixed, leaving no discretion to the judge to reduce it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: By section 1029 of the Criminal Code, the magistrate is empowered to impose a penalty within the limit fixed, and that section is interpreted as entitling the magistrate to impose any penalty not exceeding the penalty in the section.
Does the minister mean that the magistrate could impose a fine of less than $500?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Then why not say in
this clause, ' not exceeding $500?' Some of the magistrates do not know all the provisions of the Code, and they wouid take this section alone and say they had no discretion to fine less than $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The words, ' not exceeding $500,' might make this section more clear, I admit; but there are a number of existing sections in the' Criminal Code which proceed after the same method as this. If we were to add the words ' not exceeding ' in this section, it might be supposed that we differentiated it from the other sections, and that where these words did not appear, there was no discretion given a magistrate but to impose the maximum penalty. If the idea suggested by my hon. friend had been adopted as the general rule in the Criminal Code, it would have been the better way.

I am pretty certain that some magistrates will not know they have discretion to impose less than the maximum penalty, under the reading of this section. As to the penalty itself, as a rule it is not the rich who desert their families, and those who do could hardly pay a fine Mr. GERMAN.
of $500, so it would mean imprisonment for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I know it is a very
violent assumption, but everybody, including magistrates, is presumed to know the law.

Does the hon. minister
not think that the maximum is a little large?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think so.

I beg to draw the hon. minister's attention to the fact that the section reads. 'not exceeding one hundred dollars.' Why should any distinction be made between section 12 and section 14, which imposes a fine of five hundred dollars? If a magistrate is to interpret that to mean that he can impose a fine of five hundred dollars as the maximum, and that he can inflict any fine up to that, I think that the sections ought to read alike. If a section reads, 'not exceeding one hundred dollars,' I understand that in practice the magistrate is limited to from one dollar up to one hundred dollars. In section 14 the language is different, and I should say that the magistrate would have no discretion whatever.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think both sections should read alike. The reason the words 'not exceeding' are in section 12 is because they were already in the section, and we altered simply what was required to be altered. I think it would be better to strike the words out of section 12 rather than to put them into the other section, because we must remember that these will be sections in the entire criminal code.

I think the hon. minister will find that the term 'not exceeding' is the more common one, running through all criminal legislation. I would have no objection to this section if it were to be interpreted by the higher courts, hut it is placing jurisdiction in the hands of a magistrate, who is not apt to read a number of sections and draw inferences.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have not gone through the whole Criminal Code and put myself in a position to determine which form of expression is most frequently used; but it seems to me that, once we know that in some sections, at all events, the words 'not exceeding' are not used, it is better for us not to insert them in particular sections, because this might give strength to the suggestion that where they are not inserted the magistrate has to impose the maximum penalty., I turn up the Criminal Code and find section 415, which reads clear as follows:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to seven year's imprisonment, Ac.

According to section 1029, that is quite clear.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	My hon. friend finds
himself there in a higher court. In that case I have no objection to make. I do not feel so safe, however, when you are putting jurisdiction in the hands of a magistrate.

That is my contention.
When you go before a magistrate or a justice of the oeace who is not very conversant with the Criminal Code, there may be a danger of his not interpreting the section correctly and thinking that he has to impose the maximum penalty. If the hon. minister goes through the different sections rf the Code, he will find many sections that contain the words 'not exceeding.' Will the hon. minister not insert the words in this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I hesitate to do it without first going through all the sections and seeing what the effect would be. When we have a clear statement of law on the matter why do hon. members assume that a magistrate will read this section, and not read section 1029? If I were quite sure that I would run no risk of creating doubt in regard to a large number of other sections, I would have no objection to inserting the words ' not exceeding ' in this section. I submit, however, that, when we have a perfectly clear rule in the law itself, it is not wise for us. because we are afraid that with regard to this section the magistrate will not know the rule, to put something in this section that will make him feel justified in refusing to apply the rule to other sections where the words ' not exceeding ' are not used.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	I always understood
section 1029 to apply to the higher courts. I may be mistaken, but I never knew it to be invoked in a magistrate's court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think it has a general application. It forms part of part 20 of the Code, which is entitled ' Punishment, fines, forfeitures, costs, and restitution of property.' The first section of it says:
In the sections of this part relating to suspended sentence, unless the context otherwise requires, ' court ' means and includes any superior court of criminal jurisdiction, any judge or court within the meaning of part XVI.
Under the heading of ' Punishment generally ' are sections 1027 and 1028, which do not bear upon this. Then comes section 1029 and its terms are absolutely general. (Reading):
Whenever a fine may he awarded or a penalty imposed for any offence, the amount of such fine or penalty shall, within such limits, if any, as are prescribed in that behalf, he in
the discretion of the court or persons passing sentence or convicting, as the case may be.
Mr. MeKENZIE:	There are no limits
here at all. There is no maximum nor minimum; there is only a certain amount given. I think my hon. friend will find that section 1029 has .particular reference to cases where the magistrate can go to either extreme; but here he has no discretion at all; he is told he must impose a fine of a certain amount. My hon. friend may be perfectly right, but I think he will find that as regards summary proceedings in a court, the legislation says:	a fine not exceeding a certain amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There is no doubt it
would be better that all the sections should have the same form. As some of the sections use the words ' not exceeding,' it becomes less objectionable to insert them here, but we are adding still one more section to those which may be invoked as creating a suggestion that section 1029 does not apply to the case with which we aTe dealing, and the magistrate will say:	In
everv other case where there is only a sum mentioned. I shall and will impose the maximum penalty. The hon. member for Cape Breton North (Mr. McKenzie) says there is no limit. There is no limit downwards, but there is a limit upwards, and all that section says is that the offender shall be liable to a penalty of $200, and if he is liable to a penalty of $200, he is liable for every one of the dollars that make up $200.
On section 15-husband and wife: theft while living apart:
There might be some difficulty in identifying the property carried away by the deserting husband or wife.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It will be on the prosecution to prove that the property belongs to the person claiming it. 'If they fail to prove that they will not be able to secure a .conviction.
On section 16-false statements in writing:

This is a very dangerous
clause to add to the Criminal Code. It seems to me that it is giving power to a magistrate or court that ought not to be placed in such hands, and is making a criminal offence of that which is well known now simply to be the subject of civil action. I am personally opposed to turning our police courts and criminal courts of justice generally in collecting agencies for commercial purposes. In my experience at the Bar, I have found that some of our magistrates are not capable of distinguishing between a statement made in good faith and one made with the intention of committing fraud. Take the Sub-section:

(b) Knowing that a false statement in writing has been made respecting die financial condition or means or ability to pay, of himself, or sneh person, firm or corporation in which he is interested, or for whom he is acting, prpcures upon the faith thereof, either for the benefit of himself or such person, firm or corporation, any of the benefits mentioned in paragraph (a) of this section.
Many a merchant gives a statement to his banker in perfect good faith as to his ability to pay, and six months afterwards the charge may be laid against him that at that time he committed a fraud and is liable to punishment under this section. It seems to me this legislation is going very far and that it would be well for this Parliament to proceed very cautiously in making this a criminal offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will notice that the essential thing to this being a criminal offence is that the falsehood should be known to the person who makes the statement or seeks to benefit by it. It is one thing to make a mistaken statement and another to make a false statement. As the law stands at present, if a man obtains goods by false pretences, he is guilty of an offence, and it is no easier, when dealing with a case of that kind to prove that the man knew the falsity of the statement he was making than in this particular case, I do not see any reason to apprehend that because the making of the false statement is made an offence-not merely the actual procuring of goods-that there is any greater danger, that a man who did not knowingly make a false statement will be convicted than there is under this Act of a man who procures goods by a false statement. In both [DOT]cases it will be on the prosecution-to prove that there is a statement made that is knowingly false. These two section have *been asked for by numerous boards of trade, -and especially pressed for by the credit men's association of Canada which is an incorporated body composed of the credit men of practically all the wholesale firms of this country who ft.id that they are placed in this position: Men make false statements of their assets and liabilities, for instance, showing a solvent condition. They hand them in to different commercial agencies in whose charges they may be scrutinized more or less carefully. On the strength of that they get credit and goods are sold to them. The only difficulty under these circumstances of obtaining a conviction is that you cannot prove the direct communication of the false statement to the man who sells the goods, but the practical result is precisely the same as though the accused had walked into the shop, presented his false statement and on the strength of it got the goods. This section will go no further than the punishment of a man who knowingly makes a false statement with a Mr. FRIPP.
view to thereby obtaining goods, or cash, or credit; and further to make liable to punishment the man who knowing that a false statement of that kind has been made on his own behalf, or on behalf of some firm or corporation or .company in which he is interested or for whom he is acting, avails himself of the false statement that was made for the purpose of procuring the actual delivery of goods. For my part, I cannot connect this change in the criminal law with providing a means to collect civil debt by means of the criminal law. What is going to be punished here is the false and fraudulent statement that a man made, and that alone. It can hardly be said that when you provide a penalty for stealing, you provide a method by which a man may be frightened into paying back what he stole, and that you are thereby providing a means to enforce a civil obligation. There is no doubt that out of every fraud there arises a civil obligation to indemnify the party defrauded, but it does not necessarily follow that there may not 'be sufficient reason to make a criminal offence of certain methods by which fraud is perpetrated, and that is all this legislation proposes.
