On section 24-arrest without warrant for procuring:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This adds to the cases in which persons may be arrested without a warrant, the persons being offenders against section 216 that we passed this afternoon, defining offences in connection with what is generally called the white slave traffic and the procuring of women for prostitution. The necessity of getting a warrant, it has been found, has facilitated numerous escapes. Men are observed under circumstances where there is conclusive, or at all events, very strong, reason to' believe that they are engaged in taking females from one place to another for immoral purposes, and officers have been powerless because they have to get a warrant.
On section 25-summons or warrant for witnesses:
What is the change ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Section 655 of the
Criminal Code was amended in 1909 so as to provide that the magistrate, when a complaint is laid before him, may hear witnesses. It seems that this has been interpreted as imposing upon him the obligation to hear witnesses. The amendment

merely provides that when a complaint is made the magistrate may, if he considers it desirable or necessary, hear witnesses. This is to make it clear that he is not bound.
On section 26-depositions in writing or by stenography:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The only change is that where there is an official court stenographer, who has been sworn to accurately report and transcribe the evidence, it shall not be necessary for him to testify under oath that in the case of each deposition the transcription is correct.

It is hardly worth
while to amend the Criminal Code for such a slight change. It is desirable to leave the code alone as much as possible and not to make changes except where it is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In large centres like Montreal, where there is an official sworn stenographer, it adds very greatly to the work if he has to make a separate affidavit for each deposition. Where you have a large number of cases, and where you have a stenographer or stenographers to the court who are officials and who are sworn to transcribe the depositions correctly, you save a good deal of time and a considerable amount of inconvenience by this amendment.
On section 27-notice of appeal:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The changes that are affected by this section are two in number. In the first place, there is a provision made for a surety justifying under oath of the sufficiency of his bond. But the principal change is that application for admission to bail pending an appeal must be made to the justice who pronounced the conviction. If refused, the application may be made to the judge of the court to which the appeal is directed. If it is impossible to get it from the justice who pronounced the conviction, then application may be made to the judge of the court directly to whom the appeal will go, or in the province of Quebec, except in the districts of Montreal and Quebec, to any judge of the Superior Court. The evil that is sought to be remedied is that persons convicted of offences under the portion of the code which deals with the summary trial of indictable offences may take an appeal, and may then apply to practically any justice for bail. They may apply to a county court judge, the clerk of the peace, a justice of the peace or the clerk of the county court before which the conviction has been made. It has been found that under that system there has been considerable abuse. These people have gone to some justice of the peace
who has no information concerning the case, and. in many cases they have been admitted to bail, where a man knowing all the circumstances probably might have refused it. The particular instances which have made it seem desirable to legislate in this matter have arisen in the city of Montreal, and particularly in the case of prosecutions for keeping bawdy houses. Under this system, when a conviction has been obtained, bail has been put in before some one of these officers, frequently valueless bail has been accepted and the prisoner has disappeared before the appeal came on. This is to ensure that under the circumstances substantial bail shall be obtained.
Mr, McKENZIE:	While there is no
doubt such evils as those which the minister has described should be provided for, this amendment is going to create a good deal of trouble in some parts of the country. Take a case that every lawyer in the province of Nova Scotia meets with. I may go with my client twenty or twenty-five miles to a magistrate in a remote isection of the country in order to have a case tried, and find that the magistrate reserves his decision until the next day or maybe a -week afterwards. I get notice that he has given a conviction against my client, with which I am not satisfied and from which I desire to appeal. Under former conditions I could send my notice of appeal, complete my bonds right in the town in which I live, file them in the regular way and the magistrate would be obliged to send the papers to the Court of Appeal. As my hon. friend proposes to amend the law, I or my client would be obliged to go a distance of twenty or twenty-five miles to that magistrate and then perhaps find that he refuses to accept a bond. I would then be put-to the trouble of going to a higher court. If it is possible to confine this new remedy to the cities, 1 would suggest to my hon. friend that it is desirable to do so. It would not work any great hardship in a city like Montreal where all the parties are, as a rule, confined to the city. In the country districts it would work a very great hardship.

The point made by. mv bon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenziel is very well taken so far as the country districts are concerned. There is another point in connection with this section; sub-section iv of clause (c) says:
Upon making a deposit of the fine or costs or entering into recognizance, as the case may he, such appellant shall he liberated from custody.
Sub-section 1 of clause (c) says:
If the appeal is from a conviction or order adjudging imprisonment, the appellant shall

either remain in custody until the appeal is heard by the court to which the appeal is given or shall enter into a recognizance as hereinafter provided; or, if the appeal is from a conviction or order whereby a penalty or sum of money is adjudged to be paid, the appellant shall "deposit the amount of such fine with the justice, together with such further amount as the justice deems sufficient to cover the costs of the appeal, or shall remain in custody until the appeal is heard by the court to which the appeal is given or shall enter into a recognizance as hereinafter provided.
Sub-section iv might mean the costs of the justice who convicts. For instance, a fine of $20 and costs of $4.50 is imposed. That would mean that the appellant would have to deposit $24.50 before he would be liberated. According to sub-section 1, the costs of the appeal might be $10. There seems to be a conflict between these two sub-sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think it would be difficult to make it perfectly clear. The intention certainly is that the appellant shall deposit the sum that it is declared necessary to deposit. I would he willing to adopt any form of words that would make the matter clear. I might say ' the deposit above provided for.'
All right.

I wish seriously to impress upon the ' minister the advisability of leaving the law as it is at present, and of providing by some substantive section for such cases as are brought to his attention. It would meet the necessity and avoid the chaos that would be created in the country districts by this radical departure from the practice of appeals from magistrates' courts.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the law at present, a man who has been convicted before one justice may start out and hunt up some other who does not know anything about the circumstances and who possibly is in no good position to appreciate what would be sufficient bail. I apprehend the difficulty suggested by the hon. member. Would it be met if we gave to the man convicted the option of going to the county court judge instead of to a justice of the peace. The law at present gives too wide choice to a convicted person to find his own justice to take the recognizance.

I never knew of a
case in my own province, in my experience of twenty years' practice at the Bar, where any abuse arose because of that privilege extended to the man convicted. In civil matters, the law formerly was that you had to go before the magistrate who tried the case, but that was found to be a great hardship and the legislature changed the law, Mr. CARROLL.
so that you may now in civil cases complete bonds before any justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps it would meet the objections of the hon. gentleman if the law were allowed to stand as it is, with a provision added prefixing the words: Where the conviction has been pronounced in a city or town?

That would be very
much better. My object 'is to provide against obliging a man to travel long distances. You might add the words: Where the cause of action arose and the case tried and conviction obtained in a city or town.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There might be difficulty in ascertaining where the cause of action arose.

Suppose a North Sydney man is taken to Louisburg thirty-five miles away to be tried for an alleged offence, and he is convicted by the magistrate there,, he is then sent to the jail at Sydney which is twenty-five miles nearer, but still ten miles away from his home. He would have to go back these twenty-five miles _ to Louisburg to make application for bail, instead of going to his own town where he is known and could get his bondsmen all the time he remains in the custody of an officer. Under the old system he could send for two bondsmen to his old home and go before a magistrate in the vicinity of the jail. Tremendous confusion is capable of being created by this amendment.

There is much in what has been said by the hon. member. The suggestion that the man convicted should go before a judge of the county court would not be convenient in the maritime pro-mces, where the judge may live one hundred miles away from the locus in quo. In Ontario they have two judges for most of the counties, and in Quebec you have one judge for each judicial district, while the suggestion to go before the county court judge might suit in these provinces, it would not suit in the maritime provinces. I would suggest that the appeal be given to the police magistrates who are located in the towns and who are a very respectable class of men in the maritime provinces. I think he will meet the objection of my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and yet place every person in as good a position as they ought to be placed in in order to prosecute an appeal. Perhaps the minister would not feel like making the change, but I wish he would at least consider that phase of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is not the desire at
all to create a situation under which a person fairly entitled to appeal shall be put under any hardship. I confess, I did not realize the difficulties that have been referred to.

If the minister would
pardon me, I would like to make another suggestion. The hon. gentleman has never practised in tile country, and does not know what we have to contend with. In many cases the county magistrate is counsel for the plaintiff, and if the plaintiff comes before him, he feels it his duty to make a conviction, and having made the conviction, does not wish to go back on his client, and will hesitate before he will grant an appeal. That does not apply to police magistrates; they take a broader view of the case. I am afraid the hon. minister is making it almost impossible for a man to appeal. It may be that he ought not to have the right to appeal, but if he is given the right, no obstacles should be placed in his way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would it meet the hon. gentleman's view if this were confined to convictions taking place in cities, or, possibly towns? The evil sought to be remedied which has been very pronounced, is so far as I know, principally confined to the city of Montreal. You see we have numerous-I might almost say innumerable-justices of the peace, and even among justices of the peace there are some people who are not exceedingly scrupulous. Take the case particularly of a woman convicted of keeping a bawdy-house. These women go before a practically unknown justice, and enter into the recognizance with a couple of their friends, 'and the first thing the convicting magistrate knows, they are out of jail, and that is the last that is seen of them. I want to meet that situation; at the same time, I do not want to do wrong to people situated in the position suggested. It seems to me that we might meet the requirements on both sides if we let the law stand generally as it is, and enacted these two clauses, while inserting some such provision as 'when the conviction has been pronounced in a city.'

Will the hon. minister
add ' ot town ' ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am trying to find
the form of words that-
And better add 'or incorporated village,' because in Ontario we have many incorporated villages in which there is a police magistrate.

The amendment will
greatly' improve this new Bill. At the same time it scarcely covers the objection taken by my hon. friend from Cape Breton North. Take that county in which we both reside. We have perhaps eight or nine incorporated towns, some of them forty or fifty miles apart. If the conviction takes place say in Louisburg of a man belonging to North Sydney, the amendment would not allow the police
magistrate of North Sydney to accept the recognizance in this instance,. and the police magistrate in Louisburg might not know whether tire sureties offered were men of straw or good men, not knowing the locality from which the alleged criminal came. If some amendment could be made that would give police magistrates in any town the right to take bail for any person convicted in any part of the same county, the difficulty would be overcome.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps we might let the clause stand. I will see if I can find some formula that will meet the justice of the case, and at the same time attain the object which we seek to attain.

Why is it necessary to make the change in the law? I do not agree with the hon. member for Garleton (Mr. Carvel!) that the justice of the peace is counsel for the prosecutor. So far as the province of Ontario is concerned, our justices of the peace are as absolutely impartial, so far as my experience goes, as the judge on the bench. I have never found they were acting as counsel for the prosecutor. But I cannot see why the minister desires to make the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I endeavoured to point that out some time ago. We want to prevent people who have been convicted from picking out some justice of the peace who knows absolutely nothing of the circumstances of the case and making their application before him to put in the recognizance provided for.

They should not be
allowed to do so, and I never heard they did.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Under the present law they do. The recognizance may be put in before any justice of the peace, and it does work out that people pick out a justice of the peace-not that he is necessarily dishonest or unreasonable or does not want to be impartial, but that he may be an ignorant man, and in many eases when he is not generally speaking an ignorant man, he is apt to be selected by reason of unfamilarity with the nature of the offense and of the people-their one object being to get in the recognizance. These people do not turn up for their appeals; they escape. In the city of Montreal, it is no exaggeration to say, this has become a crying evil.
I do not know why, when a person is sent up for trial by the magistrate-	.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This is not the case of a man who has gone for a preliminary inquiry and has been sent up for trial, but

1162ft
of the man who has been sentenced and convicted.
Summarily.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, summarily; and
he has the right to appeal, and he remains in custody unless he gives the recognizance in question. The law provides that he-
-shall enter into a recognizance in form 51 with two sufficient sureties, before a county judge, clerk of the peace, or justice of the peace for the county in which such conviction has been made, conditioned personally to appear at the said court, and to try such appeal, and to abide the judgment of the court thereupon, and to pay such costs as are awarded by the court; and upon such rerecognizance being given, the justice before such recognizance is entered into, shall liberate such person, if in custody.
Then I think he should enter the recognizance before the justice of the peace convicting him.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is the provision I am trying to make, and I will give him the opportunity, if he cannot go to that justice of the peace, to go to somebody else. I am giving him also the right of appeal, as it were, from the refusal of that justice of the peace; all I am requiring is that in the first instance he should go to that justice. Possibly we might get at this in a more satisfactory way if we defined what constitutes inability to go to that justice. I should think that in the majority of cases the man is before the justice when he is convicted. No doubt there may be some inconvenience under the law as proposed, but on the other hand the law as it exists is certainly exceedingly faulty in so far as the condition of affairs to which I have alluded exists.

It seems to me that the minister should redraft this clause for the purpose of carrying out the principle which he suggests,, namely, that it shall apply to cities and incorporated towns and villages. I am satisfied that if this were done the requirements of the maritime provinces would be met. There is no doubt that in many instances decisions are given by the magistrates before the accused, but in the country districts the parties concerned do not always get full justice in this regard. As the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) pointed out, in many cases great hardship results from the fact that the justices of the peace do not like to decide these cases in the presence of the accused; they" usually look as learned as pos-* sible, take time to consider the matter, and then give their decision.

As I have pointed out, it is sometimes necessary to go twenty, thirty or forty miles to appear before a magistrate who is to try the case. Very Mr. DOHERTY.
often he reserves his decision, and two or three days afterwards we find that he has given a decision with which we do not at all agree. That means that we have to retraverse the forty miles in order to file a bond before him, taking our bail with us. If he is convinced that his own conviction would be sustained, he does not accept our bail bond; then we have to go back over the same forty miles, perhaps returning with another two men, whose sureties he may also refuse to accept. We may then endeavour to persuade a county court judge that the man should be given bail. I have said in the presence of the hon. Minister of Justice that I have never known of a case where this privilege was abused in Nova Scotia. The principle followed in our province is that the right to appeal should be made as easy as possible, and that no impediment should be placed in the way of a man's getting to a higher court. To give a magistrate the power to refuse an appeal is giving him a power he should not have. I am sorry I cannot say for the magistrates in my own province what the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) said about the magistrates in the province of Ontario. We have in our province many magistrates who practise as a profession, and they are not at all generous about granting appeals and giving the higher court an opportunity to reverse their decisions. I must protest as strongly as possible against any change whatever being made in the law as it is now. I submit to the minister that if there are cases for which he must provide, he should provide for them by substantive sections dealing specifically with those cases, and leaving the law as it is. As the law stands it is all right, and the addition of substantive clauses will remove the difficulty with" which the minister has had to contend in large cities.

Has the minister considered the advisability of changing the whole method of appeal? I know I could not ask the minister to accept my suggestion to'-night, but I want him to think it over. Under the law as it now stands, an appeal is really not an appeal at all; it is a re-trial. You file your bonds, go before the county court judge and bring up and re-examine all the witnesses, together with any new ones, if you can get them, and really it is a re-trial of the case. I have always thought that this is a rather cumbersome and expensive proceeding, and I think contrary to the general principles of the administration of justice in the lower courts. I have often thought that we should have what we- call the review system, by which a civil case is taken up from a lower court to a higher court in the form of an appeal, and the judge of the higher court having the record	of

the case as tried in the lower court before him, has the right to consider the whole case and decide according to the very right of the matter. If some such systerp could be devised regarding appeals in criminal matters, it would be much more satisfactory than the present system, and if the record of the lower court went up to the higher court, the judge could deal with it and decide the case according to the rights thereof. I think we would get better justice under this system, and that much of the expense and delay and inconvenience of getting these matters before the higher courts and getting an opinion upon them would be dispensed with.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We have had before us in the department many suggestions which are not acted upon in the amendment now before us. We realize that there is a wide field for improvement in the Criminal Code, and I hope that some time we shall be able to take it up and deal with it in a more general way, and when that time comes I shall be glad to consider the suggestion of my hon. friend, together with any others he may offer. With regard to this particular section, as I am not in a position to say offhand that there may not be cases such, as those to which my attention has been called, and_ inasmuch as the session is drawing to a' close, I am disposed to drop the latter portion of this section for the present, and to allow to stand simply the amendments to paragraph b of article 750, to which no objection has been taken, and to which I do not think any can be taken. When a party appeals it is required that he give notice to the respondent or to the magistrate. This amendment. modifies that by prescribing that he shall give notice to both. I would move that section 27 be amended by making the verbal changes necessary to express this meaning.
On section 29-appeals in certain cases:

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The change here is to
restore the law to the condition in which it was prior to the revision of the statutes in 1906. The practical effect is to provide that when a party is convicted under clauses ' e ' and ' f ' of section 773 of the Criminal Code of theft of an amount under $10, or of the offence of keeping a disorderly house under section 228, and the trial, is had under Part XVI, there shall be no appeal save in the case where his trial is before two justices of the peace. Wherever he has been tried before a magistrate or a judge of a higher court there shall be no appeal.
On section 31-deposition on preliminary inquiry may be read in evidence in certain events: *

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The effect of this
amendment is to add to the cases in which
the deposition on preliminary inquiry may be read in evidence, the case in which a witness at the preliminary inquiry, where there has been full opportunity of crossexamination at that inquiry, refuses to be sworn or to answer questions in a subsequent proceeding. One case of this kind that has arisen was in connection with a charge of incest, where a daughter gave evidence on the preliminary inquiry, but on the subsequent inquiry refused to give evidence.
That is a law that I think it is recognized in jurisprudence may be capable of producing collusion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It is only in cases
where there has been full opportunity for cross-examination in the court below.
But there must be full opportunity in any case, because there could be no preliminary inquiry if the prisoner were not present. Therefore, under any circumstances, this evidence will be admissible.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Just as it is to-day in regard to a witness we cannot find or a witness who is unable to be present. The only change is that under the conditions subject to which a deposition may be taken-

These are the same as
at the present time?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These are all the same but we add one more reason for allowing the deposition to be used and that is when the witness refuses to give evidence.

Refusal to answer is
contempt of court. Our law, both civil and criminal, provides that a person who refuses to give evidence is guilty of contempt of court. Is this witness to escape the penalty for contempt of court?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, the witness will be prosecuted just the same but we have the evidence. Under the system at present you punish the witness but you do not get the evidence. You get the evidence under this proposed amendment but you do not prejudice your right to punish the witness. The ends of justice will not be defeated because the witness refuses to answer.

But a statement by
any person is not evidence while he is subject to contempt of court. Until he purges his contempt, whatever he may say in the course of the inquiry, is not evidence. Thus, a party may continue for a year in contempt and under the common law anything he has said will not be evidence because he has not purged his contempt.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Even anything he said before he was guilty of contempt? This amendment is for the purpose of taking the

evidence, given subject to cross-examination and preventing the person who is in contempt of court by his own contempt, from defeating the ends of justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Then I will have to

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The legislature of Quebec has provided that the judge of the district of Beauharnois shall reside in the city of Montreal, and we are providing he shall be paid the salary which is paid to a judge appointed to the district of Montreal, with residence in Montreal. Attached is the condition, that the judge of the district of Beauharnois, being resident in Montreal, shall devote all of his time not required for the service of the district of Beauharnois to the performance of judicial duties in the city of Montreal;

There is a proposition which will shortly be brought before the Bar of Quebec, that all the judges shall reside in Montreal or Quebec, except those appointed to the districts of Ottawa, Montcalm, and Pontiac. Perhaps the minister should wait until he sees what decision is come to on that question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: In the particular case of the district of Beauharnois, the Quebec Government has moved one step in the direction of uniting the judges in Montreal, and by this legislation we make clear our approval of that action. Personally I would prefer that the centralization of the judges should be done in a general way, but those familiar with the past history of this question in Quebec realize the difficulties surrounding any government which undertake to centralize the judiciary. There are strong prejudices against that system. For my own part, I should think it would be eminently desirable.

Last year the judges of
Montmagny and Beauce were authorized to reside in Quebec; this year the judge of Beauharnois is authorized to reside in Montreal and some years ago the judge for Terrebonne was also so authorized. You are centralizing them piece-meal, but it would be much better to do it under some general legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: For my part I endorse what the hon. member says. I have not the power to bring that about, and apparently the Government of the province which has the power does not consider it possible to do so,, even though it should so desire.

Do I understand that the Minister of Justice would favour such a change in the judicial system of the province of Quebec as would bring all the judges of that province to reside at Montreal and Quebec and leave the rest of the province absolutely without judicial representation? I am not sure that such a scheme would work satisfactorily. For my part, I would agree to introduce into Quebec the system of Ontario, under which there would be county court judges in the different districts, and superior court judges in Montreal and Quebec. But, since we have not the Ontario system, I think it would be very unfortunate if all the judges were to 'be brought to the cities of Montreal and Quebec, and the rest of the province left without judicial representation. For example, does the Minister of Justice believe that the cities of Sherbrooke, Three Rivers and St. Hyacinthe should be without resident judges? I believe we have too many judicial districts in the province of Quebec; but unless there is some radical change which would approach the Ontario system, the bringing of the judges into the
'two largest cities of the province will never be satisfactory. I can quite understand the reason for this special exception made with reference to Beauharnois, because Beauharnois is now at the very door of Montreal, and while the judge resides in Montreal, he can give all the necessary time to the judicial work of his district.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I did not intend to
suggest that all the judges of the province should Teside in Montreal or Quebec. I think it would be better to call it a grouping of the judges in the different cities of the province, rather than centralization in the two largest cities. If I were called upon to deal with the question, I certainly would consider the point raised by my right hon. friend. I believe, however, that if more of the judges were brought into the city of Montreal, it would be of great advantage to the administration of justice. I would not suggest that we should bring a judge from a remote district to reside in Montreal; but there are a number of judicial districts in the immediate vicinity of Montreal, of which Beauharnois is one, and where the judicial business is not very heavy and could be done quite as conveniently .if the judges for those districts were residents of Montreal. The situation to-day is that we have to take the rural judges into Montreal, and their residence being fixed by the provincial authority in different towns around Montreal, when they come to Montreal an extra allowance has to be made them. I quite agree that if all the judges were brought into the cities of Quebec and Montreal, it would probably necessitate the adoption of the county court judge system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Wherever the circumstances may call for it, I shall be glad to bear in mind the desirability of providing a Judge who speaks both languages. I am very much disappointed that the hon. minister has not seen Mr. PROULX
his way clear to provide for increased salaries to county .court judges in the maritime provinces. I have discussed this matter pretty fully both this session and last. Great injustice is being done to these gentlemen, who are in a different position from the county court judges of the rest of Canada. They occupy important positions, and they have to travel over large circuits, from one hundred to one hundred and twenty miles in length. It is a pity that my hon. friend does not see his "way clear to remunerate these men properly.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend is more disappointed than I am that it is not possible for me to deal with this matter at this session. We must endeavour to deal with these salaries in some uniform way, or at all events to base ourselves upon some common principle. In the time at my disposal, I found the difficulties in the way of doing that insuperable. I do not want to go into a discussion on the subject; but the positions of the judges in the different provinces vary in so many respects that it is difficult to arrive at a uniform figure that would be just. Some provinces have more judges than they need; some perhaps have not as many as they need; in some provinces judges have sources of earning power which they do not have in other provinces. All these matters require to be adjusted. Before next session I propose to do my best to induce the authorities of the different provinces to endeavour to see what may be' done to bring about a more uniform condition of things. If I can get that done, I shall be glad to act. If, after making my best efforts, I cannot get that d'qne, I shall act, but I shall have tb act as best I can under existing circumstances.

Those of us who are-interested in this question of relieving the anomaly in regard to the remuneration of county court judges in the maritime provinces will be gratified to hear the assurance of the hon. minister that he is considering the matter, and that at a subsequent session he will be able to deal with it. I am quite sure the hon. minister knows that a condition exists that requires a remedy. I hope he will be able to deal .with it at the next session of Parliament.
In connection with the resolutions generally, I can see the reason why there-should be some change in the remuneration paid to judges for attending court at places other than their place of residence. But' when the minister is increasing thatr amount, I do not think it should be limited to cases where the judge is sitting in a city, as apparently is the effect of this-clause (j). I have in mind the case of the judicial district to which I belong. It is made up of .two very large counties, Pictou

and Cumberland. The county town is Amherst which, according to the status fixed in some of the provinces might be classed as a city, and yet in the legal sense it is not so regarded. The learned judge who presides in that district goes to Amherst to hold court, and I am sure the additional expense involved in going to a town like Amherst is as great as in the case of many places technically known as cities under the provincial law. I think it is hardly worth while, when making the increase, to make so fine a distinction, and I would urge upon the minister, seeing that generally he is not dealing with the judges' salaries-that being still in prospectu-he might make this increase of ten dollars absolute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is not designed to be a remuneration for services, but an allowance for expenses. Generally speaking the judge is allowed $6 besides his cost oi transportation. I think it is within the knowledge of all of us that the judge, or any other man, going to a small town or village will probably not find a hotel that will relieve him of his $6 to take care of him for a day. But when the judge goes to one of our large cities, like Toronto, Montreal or Ottawa, unless he puts up at a second class hotel, he cannot get through on less than $10 a day. If this be applied to the. smaller towns and villages, you give judges in effect additional remuneration. I do not say the judges should not have additional remuneration, but I think that if they are to have it they should be given it directly as such.

This is so much abused
by some judges. I know a judge who draws travelling allowances to which he is not entitled, making his own certificate. I have drawn this matter to the attention of the Department of Justice and they are ready to accept the certificate of the judge. But I know the certificate is false.

I would urge the necessity of considering the readjustment of the salaries of the supreme court judges of the province of Alberta relatively to those of other provinces in Canada. The remarks of the hon. member for Carleton apply to the district court judges in the proviiice in which I reside. A salary of $3,000 in New Bruns* wick, I know from observation, is worth much more than $3,000 in Alberta. I do not exaggerate when I say that $3,000 in New Brunswick must be equivalent to at least $4,500 in Alberta, yet the salary which a district court judge in Alberta receives is $3,000. The supreme court judges of Alberta are discriminated against as compared with those in Quebec and Ontario, and I think that calls for
367J
intervention by this Parliament. It would be idle for me to take up the time of the House even to mention the fact that the matter is very difficult of adjustment. There should be some basis on which we could lay down a general rule, and that rule should take into consideration jurisdiction, population, expenses of living, and other matters of that kind. I only wish to bring the matter to the attention of the-minister, and hope he will recollect that the supreme court judges in my province-are affected in this manner. So far as the allowance is concerned, I would join with the hon. member for Pictou. There are in Alberta several cities, so-called by statute, and many towns. A judge happening to go to Maeleod to hold chambers would only get the allowance for visiting a town, whereas if he goes forty miles further by railway to the city of Lethbridge, a little greater in population, he would draw the higher allowance. That is anomalous. I think it would be fairer in my province to make the allowance $10 a day or some other sum.

I think the allowance is sufficient, considering that transportation charges are paid. Of course, I understand that in a city the hotel expenses are higher. The judge gets travelling allowances cn certificate. In the province of Quebec, if he goes to the court of review, he has to have the certificate of the chief justice. There is control there, but in this case the judge sends his own certificate and there is no control. I think the judge's affidavit should accompany the certificate.

I join the hon.
members for Pictou and Carleton who _ expressed their regret that this Bill does not deal permanently with the salaries of judges. Of course, I cannot speak for any judges except those of my own province. But concerning these judges, I can say that they have no other income except their salaries. In Ontario,. I understand, judges are able to make as much again as their nominal salaries as-surrogate judges-judges of probate as we call them-masters, and in other ways. Probably the same is true of the province-of Quebec, also. But in the province of Nova Scotia there is not a cent coming to the judge of a county court except his bare salary. The only ray of hope or pleasure about this matter is that next session the minister is going to take up this subject and deal with it generally. I understand that in the province of Ontario they have two county judges for each county.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not for each count}7, but in some counties.

I am told by Ontario people that they have not work enough.

for one judge in any of these counties. In that case, one way out of the difficulty would be to superannuate one of these men and to give a decent salary to the man who remains. In Nova Scotia, we have eighteen counties, but we have only seven judges, and the minister will understand that each judge has more work than a judge in Ontario. If there is nothing that can be done in a general way for the province of Nova Scotia, one thing I wish specifically to call to the minister's attention. We have two judges in the province, of Nova Scotia who are recognized as having more work than any of the others in Nova Scotia. These are the county court judges of the city of Halifax and the judge of "the county court of Sydney. I am "sure the county court judge of Halifax will not be offended when I say that the county court judge of the city of Sydney does far more work than the other. He has a larger district and a greater population to look after, and he has to do a great deal of Supreme Court work. Halifax is the home of the judges of the Supreme Court, and the work is done by the judges themselves, but in Sydney there are no Supreme Court judges, and the judge there, as master of the Supreme Court, does an enormous volume of work-more than does the ordinary judge of the Supreme Court.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
And gets no remuneration ?	[DOT]
Mr. MoKENZIE: Not a cent.

When the county court judges were first appointed they had very slight jurisdiction in criminal matters, simply appeals, but this Parliament has imposed many duties on them as special trial judges in the criminal court, and in the county of Cape Breton an enormous volume of business is done by the county court judge. I think I am safe in saying that the county court judges in Cape Breton sit every day of the week trying civil or criminal cases. In 1905, when the present Judges Act was passed, it was agreed that the county court judges at Halifax and Sydney should receive $500 more than the other judges. The county judge of Halifax got that amount, but by some slip in the Act, the $500 for the Sydney judge was left out. I made repeated efforts to have this adjusted until I went on the bench myself, and of course throughout the three years during which I held office, I said nothing about it, but when I came to Parliament I tried to get this $500 for the gentleman who is now judge of the county court at iSyclney. It was distinctly understood that the Halifax judge and the ' 'Mr. McKENZIE.
Sydney judge should be on the same footing, and it is absolutely fair that they should be. I think it is not treating the Sydney judge fairly that this $500,should not be given to him when it is given to the judge at Halifax. Anyone who is familiar with the conditions in the province of Nova Scotia knows that it is cheaper by far to live in Halifax than in Sydney. In view of the arrangement made in 1905 that this $500 should be paid to the judge at Sydney, I think it is not fair that he should be deprived of it.

speechtext:
An additional comity

Last year when we were passing the Bill to amend the Judges' Act, I suggested to the hon. Minister of Justice an amendment to the Act having regard to the residence of the county court judges. As the law is at present, they must reside within the county or union of counties within which the courts are established. I suggested that,'an amendment should be made that the judges must reside at the county town. In, my district we are subjected to great inconvenience by reason of the fact that we have not a judge residing at the county town. The senior judge lives in Ottawa, entirely outside of the district, and he is violating the law in doing so. The junior judge lives within the district, but not at the county town. When he was appointed the senior judge was living at the county town, and it was not necessary that the junior judge should reside there, but when there is only one judge I think he should reside at the county town. Where there are two, a senior and a junior, the senior judge should reside at the county town. The county court and district judges are also local judges of the Supreme Court of Ontario, and most of the legal work is done at the county town. I would suggest that the hon. minister amend the Act" in this regard, wdth the view of providing that the county court judge shall reside at the county town, and in, districts where there are two, that the senior judge shall reside at the county town.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no .authority to deal with this phase of the matter. The Government of Canada can name, appoint and pay the judge; the. Parliament of Canada can impeach the judge, but witn regard to other matters concerning him, my hon. friend must go to the legislature of Ontario:

How was it that this
Parliament passed section 7 of the Judges Act:
'Tlie judges of the Supreme Court of Judicature for Ontario shall reside at the city of Toronto or within five miles thereof, hut leave to reside elsewhere in the province for any specified time may he granted from time to time by order of the Governor in Council.
If this Parliament could fix the residence of the Supreme Court judges why could they not fix the residence of the county court judges? The statute provides where the county court judge shall reside. In appointing a county court judge the condition is inserted in the letters patent that he shall reside in the county or union of counties for which he is appointed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Those sections, I understand, are inserted because they are in accordance with the laws of Ontario. This Parliament cannot create a power to itself by legislating about subjects which are relegated to the provinces. Under the British North America Act, this Parliament has the power to appoint judges and to pay their salaries and judges are also liable to impeachment by this Parliament, but the provincial authorities control the administration of justice and the purpose for which the judges are appointed is to administer justice. In Quebec, the province has directly and expressly legislated fixing the residence of judges.

The senior judge of Prescott and Russell, who now resides in Ottawa was appointed in 1900, and there is a condition in the patent appointing him that he must reside in the united counties of Prescott and Russell. An amendment was passed by the legislature of Ontario to the County Court Act, providing that the Lieutenant Governor in Council by Order in Council could permit a judge to reside elsewhere. Would such an Order in Council be constitutional, changing the condition of the patent appointing the judge?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not undertake to pronounce offhand on all these questions but as I understand it the legislature of Ontario has a right to say where the county court judges shall reside, and if they have that power I would understand that they have power to provide that the Lieutenant Governor in Council might fix the place of residence.

The Order in Council oi the Government of Ontario permitting the judge to reside outside the district and thereby changing the conditions of his appointment has not been passed. I believe that the Government of Ontario doubt its constitutionality and so do I. Judges are appointed for the convenience of the public, to administer justice and not to suit
their own convenience and it would be to the convenience of the constituents of my district that the judge should reside at the county town and not outside of it, so that he would be within reach of the lawyers practising in the district.

[DOT]office, will this increase date from the time of his appointment? is ,it retroactive or for the future?

Do we understand by
the word ' salary " what the judge receives -from fees and other sources besides his salary, or does this refer only to the salary paid by the Dominion?

I just wish to call the attention of the Minister of Justice, in con-Mr. OLIVER.
nection with this paragraph, to the same point I brought to his attention in connection with penitentiary officials, that the rule which permits of increased railway rates and increased bank interest to be imposed upon western people, does not seem to be applicable when it comes to paying salaries to western judges or to western penitentiary officials. (k) That to every judge of a county court who, having attained the age of 75 years, is compulsorily retired, and to any judge who, having continued in office for a period of 30 years or upwards, is compulsorily retired or resigns his office an annuity may be granted equal to the salary of the office held by him at the time of his retirement or resignation.
That changes the date of compulsory retirement from the age of 80 to 75?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

What is the reason of
the change?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has been found by
experience that gentlemen who were not possessed of the vigour that they previously had, and were consequently not as well able to perform their duties, finding that unless they stayed until they were 80, when they could be compulsorily retired, they could not retire on full pay, remained; and it has happend in some instances the administration of justice has suffered. Ws have thought that if we have the power to retire the judge at the age of 75, and his retirement will not prejudice his rights because he will retire on full pay, the public interest will be served by relieving him of further judicial duties.

This is a wise provision. While there are many men who retain their mental vigour at seventy-five or eighty years of age, yet it is not the rule. The minister ought almost to have the right to retire a judge at seventy-five years of age, if in his opinion it should be done. However, if a man were appointed at sixty-five, and retired compulsorily at seventy-five, it is a question whether he should get the full retiring allowance. I hope the minister will not appoint any men so old to the bench.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would rather bring the remedy to bear at the other end, and ap-

point them before they get to be sixty-five years.
Why does not the Minister of Justice provide for retiring Supreme Court judges, as well as County Court judges, at the age of seventy-five?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
High Court judges are entitled to retire at the age of seventy-five with full pay, if they have served twenty years on the bench. There has never been .any age fixed at which you can compulsorily retire a High Court judge.
Mr. ARMSTRONG (East Lambton) Would it not be wise?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The suggestion is worthy of serious consideration in connection with any measure dealing generally with High Court judges, and their remuneration.

There is another provision which says that judges can be retired on full pay after thirty years services. If a judge were appointed at the age of thirty-five he would be entitled to the full retiring allowance at the age of sixty-five.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The intention is to provide that a County Court judge who has served thirty years is entitled to retire with his full pay, irrespective of his age, and that is the provision which now applies to the High Court judges. When a man has served thirty years it would be undesirable to compel him to stay on for the purpose of growing old enough to get his full pay. The cases where men serve thirty years and are under seventy-five would be very rare indeed.

I think there should be a pension fund to which the judges would contribute, as is the case with the civil servants. You are making of the judges a privileged class, and there should be no privileged class in this country. In the United States they do not pay any pension to judges, and I think the principles of democracy should prevail in Canada. The [DOT]Government has an annuity system, and the judges might buy annuities under that system.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That might be considered when we come to deal in a general way with the judiciary. I suppose the hon. gentleman would not suggest that the principle he speaks of should apply to men who have already been appointed to the bench and who accepted under a law by which certain rights accrue to them. If it were decided to carry out the hon. gentleman's suggestion it would be just to take it into consideration in connection with the question of the salaries paid to our judges.	. |; I

In looking at the estimates I was struck with the great number of judges on the retired list, and to whom the country is paying a large amount annually. There were more in Quebec than in Ontario, but in Ontario one judge retired some years ago, drawing his full salary of $7,000 a year, not because he was unable to perform his duties, for he is now general manager of a trust company, and probably is receiving as large a salary as he did when actually on the bench. When a judge is permanently disabled he should have some allowance, but judges should be on the same footing as civil servants, and should contribute to a pension fund.
(l)	That the provisions respecting annuities under sections 21 and 25 of the said Act shall apply and extend to the judges of the circuit court of the district of Montreal.
What court is this?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In the district of Montreal there is a circuit court composed of three judges. Throughout the rest of the province, though the Circuit Court exists, the entire original civil jurisdiction is in the Superior Court, whether the amount be one dollar or one million dollars. In the district of Montreal it was found that the number of cases of $100 and under, which previous to the appointment of the circuit court judges were within the jurisdiction of the circuit court, presided over by judges of the Superior Court, had grown so numerous that it was impossible for the judges of the Superior Court to keep up with them. This circuit court was consequently established, and this resolution proposes to increase the number of judges by one. It is just to the circuit court judges to say that while their jurisdiction is limited to $100 in ordinary claims, they have jurisdiction in cases for the recovery of school taxes and municipal administration for a larger amount. The work of these judges is exceedingly heavy from the point of view of the number of cases that come before them.
(m)	For an additional Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Judicature for New Brun-wick, $7,000 per annum:

I want to register my protest, in as gentlemanly a manner as possible, against this. In the first place, I can see no earthly reason for an additional judge in New Brunswick. It is well known what gentleman at the New Brunswick bar will get the position, and I have no objection to him whatever. I think he is as good an appointment a3 could be made in the province. We have a population of only 350,000, and

it is not increasing very rapidly. Every member of the New Brunswick Bar knows that our judges not only are not overworked, tout have not enough work to do. The equity judges, who are now the chancery judges, are doing a large amount of work, and probably one or two others are doing a considerable amount of chamber work; but. as a rule, the six judges not only could do all the work required of them, but would be the better for having it to do. We have got as good a court in New Brunswick as any in the Dominion of Canada. It has always been of a very superior character, and its judgments are substantiated to a greater extent than any other appellate court in the Dominion. I attribute that very largely to the fact that our judges go on circuit, and also have the privilege of sitting en banc on appeal. That is what makes them the splendid jurists which they have always turned out to be. I am sorry to see a departure from that principle, which is the old English principle and which has been the principle in New Brunswick since its organization; it is also the principle in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. If the legislature of New Brunswick thought it necessary to appoint another judge, that is only a question of a salary of $7,000. Now they are creating an appeal court. Three judges will sit on appeal and four will go on circuit. The latter will never have the opportunity of sitting as an appellate court and of hearing these matters discussed. I am afraid we not only will do nothing to assist the jurisprudence in the province but will very materially reduce the standard of the judges in the future.

What my hon. friend
from Oarleton (Mr. Carvell) objects to is legislation passed by the province of New Brunswick. This Parliament has nothing to do with that; *ve have simply to provide for the salary of an additional chief justice, and to appoint a chief justice to the Supreme Court of Judicature. The legislation passed at the last session of the New Brunswick legislature was really a revival of .egislation passed some years ago when the present hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) was Prime Minister of that province. That legislation was not acted upon until this last session of the legislature, when it was re-enacted and became law.
I cannot quite agree with what my hon. friend has said with regard to the present system of judges acting on cases of appeal. The principle which my hon. friend has adduced has not been acted upon in recent years, because the judge who has tried a case does not sit in appeal on it. Therefore, he is not in a position to give his Drother judges his understanding of the witnesses and of the circumstances that Mr. CARVELL.
transpired during the trial, and they must take that from the record. Consequently I do not see any reason why the mere going on circuit would give judges any better knowledge in deciding these questions of appeal than if they sat as an appellate court, as is done in the other provinces of Canada, with the exception of Nova Scotia. Some judges are better fitted for the conduct of cases on circuit than are others. Others are better fitted to act as judges of appeal.
My hon. friend has paid tribute to the standing of the courts of New Brunswick, a tribute that is very well deserved. It has always been a splendid court, and has not taken second place to any other court in Canada.. In fact, I do not think it takes second place to the Supreme Court of Canada. By this legislation we hope not only to keep up the standard but to improve it, if we by this means give these judges an opportunity better to study up the eases on which they are to pass judgment, than if they had to go on circuit. They will only have to attend to the chancery work of the province and to the hearing of appeal cases. Therefore, upon the question of the improvement of the bench itself and from every standpoint, I think that the legislation passed by the legislature of New Brunswick is a step in the right direction, and I am glad to see that the Government is implementing it by providing the salary.

My hon. friend hardly understood the line of the argument I was making. I am quite aware that .New Brunswick has the right to create the court, and that all this Parliament has to do is appoint the judge, but this Parliament could do what they did for some two or three years in the case of Ontario, when they considered that unnecessary judges were provided for by that province; they could refuse to grant the salaries. My point is not that the appeal judge does not have the opportunity of discussing cases with his brother judges; it is the judge who goes on circuit that I am afraid will deteriorate. The judge who goes on circuit now has the opportunity of sitting in appeal on all cases except those which are against his own decision. I am safe in saying that in four-fifths of the cases that are argued before the Court of Appeal, he has the opportunity of discussing them with his brother judges. He gets the benefit of their learning. By getting together in this way they become abler and broader-minded jurists. It is the man who . does not have the opportunity of doing this that I think will not come up to the standard he has occupied in the past. I have no doubt that the three gentlemen who comprise the Court of Appeal will have probably as good opportunities to benefit them-

selves as they have at present. -But I think great benefit comes to the man who goes on circuit, and that benefit would be taken away under present conditions. Add to that the fact that we do not require a seventh judge in New Brunswick.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not rise to take part in the discussion, but as the Supreme Court o' the province of New Brunswick is being discussed, I want to tell the hon. member for Carleton that His Majesty has been pleased to bestow honour upon the head of that court, the Chief Justice. I am sure no one will be more pleased to hear it than my hon. friend.

I heard that just half
an hour ago, and I wish publicly to add my tribute to the merits of the gentleman who occupies the place of Chief Justice. No abler jurist occupies a position on the bench of any court in Canada, or, I believe, in the Empire. The distinction which has come to him he has earned by his learning and attention to business and I hope he may long be spared to enjoy the honours he has won.	' .

I congratulate the province, and the Bench, and the Chief Justice himself upon the fact that His Majesty has seen fit to confer honour upon him, an honour that is well deserved. But I would point out to the member for Carleton that the Chief Justice himself is a proof of that fact that it is not necessary for a man to go on circuit to be a great judge.
Has not the Chief Justice tried more cases in the last ten years than all the other judges in New Brunswick put together?

He has heard chancery
cases, but he has not gone on circuit.
But he has had the experience.

He has not had the slightest practice of criminal law or common law, but has been confined to chancery cases. Yet, he has proved a great common law judge as well as an equity judge. With regard to the argument that it would be a great loss to these judges not to go on circuit. 1 would remind my hon. friend that they would .still have the great advantage of hearing before them the flower of the Bar of New Brunswick of which my hon. friend is a distinguished member, which will assist them in acquiring a further knowledge of the law.

I wish to impress upon the Minister of Justice the importance of placing the Supreme Court judges in the same position as that in which he is placing the County Court judges. The Supreme Court judges who
are trying most important cases, cases in which men's lives are at stake, great industrial disputes, continue in their position until they are a hundred if they live so long and wish to continue. We have men now on the Supreme Court bench of Ontario who are eighty years of age.
And they are the best.

That may be the
hon. gentleman's opinion. I am not finding fault with men of that age; but lawyers in general do not care to take the position I am taking here on this subject. As a layman I feel free to express my opinion, and I am confident we should have an age limit in the case of the Supreme Court as well as the other.

There is no necessity for that. There are old men on the Bench of Ontario, but I do not think the profession has ever complained of their incompetency or of the manner in which they perform their duty. The Chancellor could retire on full pay if he wished to do so, but if he prefers to work, why should he be retired. I believe the pensioning of judges has gone too far; the minimum, of service of the Superior Court judges is too low. A judge can be retired on two-third salary after fifteen years' service. And in the province of Quebec men have retired who were able to continue to perform their duties. They are practieising law. One of them draws over $5,000 a year-two-thirds of $8,000. Yet he has a law office competing with other lawyers. Is it just to the members of the profession that they should be compelled to compete with a man who draws over $5,000 from the public treasury? Besides these gentlemen get a certain reputation through having been on the Bench. I think the period should be extended and judges should be pensioned only if necessary because of their age or incapacity to perform their duties.

I heard with delight the news announced by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen). The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of the province of New Brunswick holds a high position on the Bench of New Brunswick, and I think he has the confidence of everybody. The distinction is well deserved. I am sure he is to be congratulated, and more than that . the people of New Brunswick are to be congratulated upon having so distinguished a head, and of having the gentleman who is the head recognized in the fashion indicated. This is not the place to criticise legislation of the province of New Brunswick. But the legislation which was enacted some few years ago certainly did not meet with my approval, and I can only say I have not been convinced that there

was any occasion for the renewal of that Act. I think it is recognized by laymen throughout the province, by the Bench and the Bar, that the paucity of business coming before the Supreme Court arid before the court en banc has been such during the past four or five years that it is becoming a by-word and a reproach. I think it the height of absurdity to ask for an additional judge. I have no comments to make with respect to any one likely to take that position. J have heard several gentlemen named, any of whom would reflect upon the Bench; but in my_ opinion, however eminent, however qualified, nobody is required. There are -enough judges there to do the business, and the fact of the matter is that those who are there today are simply rusting out. The Chief Justice, so far as the chancery side of the court is concerned, has done a good deal of business, he and Mr. Justice McLeod. But anyone who practises in the province of New Brunswick must recognize the fact that there is hardly a circuit court meeting in any county to-day that lasts more than one or two days. In nine cases out of ten the court adjourns on the very day upon which it opens, and it is seldom that it lasts more than two or three days. It has certainly been many years since a circuit court has lasted more than a week. In the county of Westmorland, from which I come, there used to be a very heavy busi. ness before the circuit court, but to-day only a few criminal cases, ever come before it, and hardly any civil cases. I think I am not extravagant in making the statement that the judges are rusting because of the want of exercise of their powers in the trial of cases.

The conditions existing
in New Brunswick last year in that regard may be similar to those in Ontario. We voted salaries for two judges last year, for instance, and almost all the judges in Ontario said they were not needed.

As a representative of the farming community, I also, Mr. Chairman, wish to make a few remarks on the salaries of judges and on retirement allowances paid to them by the Government. It appears we have this year a surplus of 55 millions, and to hear the hon. members who have spoken during the last few days, it would seem that an effort is being made to reduce that surplus, first of all by paying the members themselves an extra indemnity of $1,000 or $1,500 each for the present session.
I will now take all of these government pensioners, and I may say that -the farming class is strongly opposed to all the high salaries we are paying.

Is the farming class
Mr. EMMERSON.
equally opposed to the ten millions we have just voted for them?

It will take ten years
to pay that amount. I am now speaking about the judges. We have in the province of Quebec fifteen judges who are receiving a pension from the Government, and that is costing us $90,500 per annum. The great province of Ontario is only having $15,000 under that head.
I take the case of a judge who resigns his position at the age of 50-for quite a number of men live to the age of 80, and even more-but let us suppose that this judge is going to live until he is 80 years' old. He will be receiving a pension during 30 years. Should his salary be $7,000 a year, that pension will be $4,666 a year. Multiply that 'by 30, and you will have the fabulous sum of $140,000 of pension. Now, add to that compound interest at 7 per cent-because I presume the judges who have resigned, not on account of sickness, but in order to keep their position in financial institutions and big estates-have resigned because they were businessmen, so that that money brings them at least 6 per cent. I therefore conclude that such a judge at the age of 80 years shall have received at least $300,000 from the Government.
I find no words to qualify such an abuse. I will take the case of the Minister of Justice himself, who is drawing in the first place a pension from the Government as a retired judge, a salary as a minister and still another as a member of Parliament. Will not the hon. minister find some means of amending the law in his own case, by abolishing his own pension at least during the time he holds his position as a minister and a member of the House?
I say that if the fanning community was posted on all these matters, they could not tolerate in power a Government under which such abuses are allowed. Farmers are the people who do the greatest amount of work. There is no pension for them and they ask for none.
Why could not a judge on the bench, with a salary of $7,000 a year, provide for his old age by means of an insurance? With such a salary it should be an easy matter for him to take an insurance of $25,000. That is just what we are doing ourselves when we join the mutual benefit societies, such as the Independent Foresters, the Catholic Foresters, and the National Alliance, for instance. Why should they not do like us and buy life annuities?
No; pensions must be paid to these gentlemen. But that is not all. Those who come down from The bench are making places for other favourites. I have been repeatedly told that it was very difficult to get judges nowadays, because lawyers were making a great deal more in their profession. I will

take the case of Mr. Simeon Beaudin, who was a candidate against me in the last election. It was currently said_ in the county that he would not accept a judgship, when he was making $100 a day with his profession. He was a candidate, and I am told that it was the present Premier who forced him to run.
What did happen after the present Government came into power?
Mr. Beaudin was appointed a judge of the Superior Court. He left his $100 per day to become a judge at a salary of $7,000 per annum.
It is said that some lawyers refuse to be appointed judges. I see on the other side of the House, and on this side, for that matter, hon. gentlemen who would be very glad to become judges to-day, and if the hon. Minister of Justice wishes to appoint them he will find enough of them to supersede the whole bench in Montreal and all through the country.
I think the hon. minister should introduce a Bill to amend this law so as to give a pension only to those judges who become incapacitated, even when they have just been appointed to the bench; but I object to the Government paying them a pension which enables them to get rich.
After all it does not cost more to feed a judge than it does to feed a civil servant. Very few are the civil servants who are getting high salaries. The hon. Postmaster General has 900 officers in Montreal only. Very few of them get as -much as $2,000 per annum, and there are quite a number who receive less than $1,000. These young men, like the judges, have their families to support, their children to educate. For them there is no pension varying from $4,000 to $8,000 per annum.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that if the people knew all those particulars, they would severely punish the Government who are perpetuating such a state of things. I am not specially blaming the present Government; I say that both parties are guilty.
It is very well known that it is the lawyers who made the laws. We, farmers, hardly dare to raise our voices here, especially during the first years. The lawyers generally join hands to out for themselves good substantial pensions after they shall have been appointed as judges.
Sir, I do not wish to take up the time of the House any longer, but I enter my protest against this abuse of taking the people's money to pay pensions to men who have absolutely no need of them.
I believe that our duty as legislators should 'be in the first place to increase the pay of the poor employees, of those who are working 300 days during the year, who never have any holidays and who, whenever they lose any time-except through sickness-also lose their salaries.
It is altogether different with a judge who happens to have a slight headache. He immediately applies to the Minister of Justice for a holiday, which enables him to take a six months' trip to Europe, and such an application is seldom refused.
And after that the lawyers in Montreal and elsewhere will say: We have not a sufficient number of judges. That may be true, but there are always two or three travelling in Europe.
I therefore say, Mr. Chairman, that next year, if the hon. Minister of Justice does not bring a remedy to this state of things during the present year, and if he is still at the head of this department, I shall introduce a Bill to amend this ill-omened law and to prevent the paying of pensions to people who have no need whatever of them and are drawing other salaries as in the case of the present Minister of Justice.
