On the motion of Hon. Mr. Crothers, Bill No. 209, to amend the Dominion Forest Reserves and Parks Act, was read a second time, and the House went into Committee thereon.
We were to have some ex-idanation of this.

There was some serious
objection to the withdrawal of those two half townships from the Riding Mountain reserve. As that is dropped out of the Bill, the principal objection is removed.
Before the Bill is agreed to, I wish. to say that on looking over the map, it seems 'o me that the Government has erred rather on the side of liberality in taking land into the forest reserves. My opinion is that there is a large amount of land in what is called the dry belt of British Columbia. which is included in the railway belt and which my hon. friend has included very liberally in additions to existing forest reserves or to new ones, that is at a very sufficiently high elevation to attract enough rain to make it suitable either for agriculture, or for grazing purposes, and should not, as a matter of sound public policy, be withdrawn from occupation. If it is an error, however, it can be remedied by subsequent legislation, and I would not desire to delay the committee more than to state my opinion.
There is also an unnecessarily large addition to the Rocky Mountain forest reserve in the territory immediately west of Edmonton. The reserve at present is very large; it has a width of about one hundred miles. To add still further to that large area is, in my opinion, questionable policy. I quite approve the policy of establishing, as forest reserve, land that is not available for settlement; but I certainly do not approve the establishment as forest reserves of land that is available for profitable occupation by settlers in large quantities, as is the case here.
It mav not be known to the Government; but as a matter of fact the low elevation of the country, which is the cause of the Yellowhead Pass being so attractive as a railway pass, extends very close to the foot

1165&.
of the mountains. There is not a very large area of foot-hill country. For that reason I do not think it is necessary or wise to give such a large extension to the eastward of the Rocky Mountain park. As in the case of the British Columbia reserve, however, that is a matter that can be adjusted by subsequent legislation.
There is one particular reserve that I wish to speak rather strongly of, that is, the reserve northwest of Edmonton, between Athabasca river and Lesser -Slave lake. There is a large area of very high land there known as Swan Hill.

What is the name of that reserve?
Mr. -OLIVER: I do not know what name is given to it. It is south of Lesser Slave lake.
There has been, no reserve there up to -the present.

I am willing to say that the area of land which we know as Swan Hills should properly be included in a forest reserve; but I am strongly of the opinion that the minister has included within that reserve an area that is entirely unwarranted owing to the elevation of the country. The country is largely timbered; but the timber is not, generally speaking, of a character to give it value. Under conditions such as prevail there, when the greater part of the land is wooded, the mere fact that this particular area is wooded is no reason why it should be set apart as a forest reserve. The only reason for setting apart as a reserve an area in a generally wooded country is if it is at such elevation, or is of such broken character that it would not be suitable for agriculture or grazing. On that ground I think the minister has erred very considerably in including an area so much larger than that which is occupied by the actually elevated country that would not in the ordinary course of events be suitable for agriculture ox grazing.
May I draw the minister's attention to the desirability, so far as it is reasonably practicable, of expanding the forest reserves on the Cypress hills? I notice that no addition has been made to that reserve. Now, if there is any one locality in the western country that calls for the attention of the forestry branch of the Department of the Interior, that calls for the establishment of a forest reserve and for forestration, it is the summit of the Cypress Hills. This is a tract of high country in the dry area of the Northwest. The ridge oi hills attracts rain which is the source of many creeks that run down to the plains on both sides of the hills. There is every reason why the Government should go to trouble and expense to expand as far as practicable the forest area on the high land of these hills-not for Mr. OLIVER.
the sake of the forest but for the sake of the water that would water the plains both to the south and to the north of the hills where water is the great necessity for agricultural occupation. By the homestead map there are still considerable areas on the Cypress hills not occupied by settlers. I would advise the minister to make closer examination of this area than has yet been made and to take means to make reservation of land there and even to buy out settlers in order to establish an important forest reserve in that locality. There is another area, one with which I am not so familiar, Woody mountain, or Wood mountain. I know that it is an elevated country, the source of water flowing both south and north, and flowing through a rather dry country. I do not know to what extent these hills are forested, never having visited them. But I think the minister would do well to have his officers visit Wood mountain. The. importance of having reservation of such portion of the area as would seem to be necessary to preserve timber, and to establish timber growth when practicable.
The value of forest preservation or forest protection, with a view to meeting the conditions of the open plains as. regards water cannot be exaggerated. It is a work which is worthy of the best attention of the Government, and while it is very largely experimental up to the present, and while we cannot measure in definite dollars exactly the result that is to follow certain expenditures, still the conditions are such that the Government is warranted in making liberal expenditures to preserve the forests now existing on these isolated prairie watersheds and protecting the forests upon them where they are adapted to such protection.
But that condition does not exist in the northern parts of the country where the country is, generally speaking, already timbered. While it is desirable that there should be proper reservations, the conditions of the prairies do not apply. I maintain that my hon. friend would not be warranted in setting apart Very large areas of forest reserves simply because the land at present is covered with timber. If the land is suited for agricultural purposes and the timber is not valuable, unless the timber is necessary as a means of conserving the water, it is not good economy to prevent the acquiring of that timber and the establishment of settlers. The principal of the forest reserve is to preserve the forests for the sake of the water supply, not simply to preserve the forests for the sake of having forest instead of field. So, when reserves are, as I understand some of -them to be in the northern country, set apart rather because the country is forested than because it is necessary to preserve the

forest in order to preserve the water supply, I think the Minister of the Interior is not in such cases following the policy that is the very basis of the Forest Reserves Act.

The general scheme
followed in setting aside these forest reserves is not to include the agricultural lands but lands that are non-agricultural. Perhaps I may, for the information of my hon. friend, give him the statement I have received from the officers who have examined these various reserves, regarding one or two of them. Take for instance, the Lesser Slave forest reserve. The information I have received concerning it is as follows:
This tract covers a range of hills with an elevation of from 3,060 to 4,000 feet. The land is rough and broken on the edges of the hills, and the summit is fiat and covered with muskeg. None of it can be classed as agricultural land. The timber is black and white spruce, lodge-pole and jack pine. Fires have at different periods run over a large part of the tract and there have been large fires within the last fifteen years; the timber grows with good, average rapidity, and this should in time be one of the most important timber areas in Alberta. With the increase of immigration into the Lesser Slave and Peace river valleys there will be a great demand for timber in the near future. There are no) settlers in this tract proposed to be included.
My hon. friend spoke of the large increase in the Rocky Mountain reserve. As to that my information is as follows:
The tract added to the east of the reserves from the North -Saskatchewan northward, is rough, broken country, traversed by deep valleys of a number of rivers. The general elevation is over 4,000 feet _ above the sea; level. In general the soil varies from sandy to clayey gumbo, the latter underlying the muskegs. This tract has suffered severely from fire. Only about eleven per cent of the area is covered by mature timber and thirty per cent by timber of pole size. The Brazeau region included in this district is estimated to contain 1,400,000,000 tons of bituminous coal, the mining of which will require about two billions cubic feet of wood for mine timbers.
That is the description of the piece that we propose to add to the Rocky Mountain reserve.

Has the minister any report on the Porcupine Hills addition to the Rocky Mountain reserve ?

There are three hundred and sixty square miles in that reserve at the present time; it is proposed to add two hundred and four square miles, making a total of five hundred and sixty-four square miles.
This reserve is marked on the map as the proposed addition to the Rocky Mountain reserve. It is in townships 9, 10, 11, 12 and 13, east and west of the fifth meridian.

The Porcupine Hills comprise an area of one hundred and ninety-eight square miles. They are separated from the main Rocky mountains by a narrow valley, and rise to a height ol between five thousand and six thousand feet above the sea level. They are-forested with spruce, Douglas fir, larch,-pine and poplar. The stand of timber is not continuous, but is good in places and natural reproduction is satisfactory. The hills are surrounded by a range of agricultural country, which is supplied with timber therefrom and which depends on the streams from the hills for its water supply.
There are quite a number of settlers in these hills, many of them farmers. Is it proposed that they shall be transferred ?
I think it is intended that, where there are settlers in any of these reserves, an arrangement will be made with them to move elsewhere.
There are quite a large number of settlers in that portion of the country known as the Porcupine Hills, Maeleod district, and I think there will be-a good deal of objection on their part to moving.

I am not personally
familiar with this locality, but as the hon.. member for Maeleod (Mr. Warnook) says, there has been a settlement there for twenty-five years. It is well established, and while not largely agricultural it is, I suppose, the best and most thoroughly established grazing area in all the West. There is agriculture accompanying the grazing, and I must say, if I am not mistaken as to the area covered, that my hon. friend is heaping up a good deal of trouble for himself in undertaking to establish a reserve covering the whole area. I am not suggesting that it would not be right and proper for him to make reservation of certain areas within that area; it is quite-possible that a careful examination would show that there are smaller areas that might possibly be reserved, but to abso-

lutely blanket six or eight townships where people have been living for twenty-five years is assuming a rather serious responsibility, and I would not like to let this section pass without entering my formal and most emphatic protest.

I have not before me any information as to the number of settlers that there may be in this district, but I do not think the officers who have personally examined the reserve, and who recommended these additions, would do so if they were aware that it was inhabited by a large number of people. In some cases a few squatters were found in some of the reserves as at present constituted and we have made arrangements with them to move to other places, and have paid them for some improvements they have made. If anything of that kind turns out, they will not be disturbed in the meantime, and an amendment may be made next year.

Some years ago every homestead or fractional part of a homestead in that part of the country was taken up. There are many ranchers and farmers in there, really mixed farmers now, who have been in there for over twenty years. They have good buildings, considerable improvements and good fences, and I think there will be a good deal of reluctance on their part to move. I certainly think that a considerable portion of this land is private property, the property of the Waldron Ranch Company. I know that their land lies pretty well on to the side of the Porcupine Hills.
I am told by the officer who has charge of the matter that there are no settlers in the portion it is proposed to add to this reserve, and that it does not include the Waldron ranch.

This information does

On motion of Hon. L. P. Pelletier (Postmaster General), Bill No. 188, to provide for more advantageous Telegraphic Communication between Canada and the United Kingdom and other parts of the British Empire, was read the second time, and the Mr. OLIVER.
House went into Committee thereon. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 1-short title:

Whilst I am quite willing to give a chance to the Poulsen Company to implement by deed what it promises by words, I cannot help saying that the Bill is a deception for all those who have favoured so far the principle of the state ownership of cables. There is no interest taken in the present measure in the country, and my hon. friend must have noticed, ever since he introduced his Bill, that the public has not been responsive. The public expected something substantial, and they get only what I call a speculative enterprise. Notwithstanding what was stated by my hon. friend when he introduced this legislation, wireless telegraphy is yet in its infancy. There is nothing final yet in this wonderful discovery. Marconi himself, the leading authority in the world, admits that there are many and many steps to be taken before this notable invention is perfected. An exhaustive investigation of the Marconi Wireless system has recently taken place in England. As my hon. friend the Postmaster General will remember, some years ago, Mr. Samuel the British Postmaster General, made an agreement with Marconi to equip all the ships of Great Britain w'ith the wireless, and he dotted the coast around the United Kingdom with stations in order to give the British navy the benefit of that wonderful invenr tion. But whilst wireless telegraphy is certainly' a great invention, which to-day in all civilized countries is obligatory upon ship-owners for the protection of lives and the safety of navigation, in the distribution of news or the transmission of messages, the cable is still the instrument which finds favour with the public. I stated the other day that the Poulsen system, excellent as it may be was somewhat criticised among the scientists and specialists in wireless. I have the evidence of Marconi himself taken only a few' days ago in London. I stated, when the minister introduced his Bill, that the trouble with this Poulsen system is that atmospheric conditions interfere with the proper working of the wireless. Mr. Marconi says in his evidence:
Lecturing before tiie Royal Institution on May 24, 1907, (copy of which lecture I have produced), Professor Fleming stated in regard to the Poulsen arc:
' No one who has worked practically with the apparatus can say that it is a simple and easy one to use. A very little want of exact adjustment causes the arc to be extinguished or ehe fluctuate greatly in current, and, compared with the extremely simple appliances required for spark telegraphy, the advantage in ease of working is largely on the si-de of the spark.'
An interesting and practical proof of the
opinions just quoted was demonstrated in a competition which was conducted by the

Turkish army in May, 1911, when the Tele-funken system, the Poulsen system, and the Marconi system were in competition tor the purpose of demonstrating which was the most efficient system for the Turkish army to adopt. Trials were carried out during a period of ten days. The Telefunken system failed to get a complete message through until the last two or three days of the trial, and then only at night time; the Marconi system maintained good communication throughout the whole period; the Poulsen apparatus failed entirely; their arc hlew out on the average once a minute. The Turkish army adopted the Marconi system.
Major Cochrane, late of the British army, was present at these trials as engineer on behalf of the Marconi Company, and I produce a letter signed by him confirming what I have stated, and he is available to corroborate in detail before this committee what I have said should he be required.
I would draw particular attention to these tests in view of the evidence which has been given before this committee, that the Poulsen system is believed to be more simple and efficient for short-distance communications. It is unnecessary for me, perhaps, to state that the first essentials for military stations are simplicity, efficiency, and reliability, and military stations such as these are short-distance installations.
Then, it goes on to deal with the various instruments. My hon. friend will probably say that Marconi is interested. Of course, his invention is decidedly the best in his own judgment, and he does not care to see Poulsen or Telefunken take precedence over him. I quoted the other day the opinion of Charles Bright who is a world-wide authority and the son of the gentleman who, some seventy years ago, laid in the Atlantic ocean the first cable and who has, during his lifetime, made a specialty of this question of telegraphy, by both cable and wireless. I would also invite my hon. friend to .read the London Times of the 8th of May last which contains a long article -on this question of wireless and which he might find useful. According to all the authorities, the cable is unquestionably the best medium for the transmission of news and messages. I shall not weary the committee by quoting at length the expressions of leading Canadians and people high in authority in England who for the last fifteen years have vainly clamoured for a state-owned cable. Although there were forebodings when the Pacific cable was established, and it was said it would not pay expenses, the fact is that there is now a surplus every year, and thete has been a steady reduction in the cable rates. These reductions have not only been valuable to the commercial world, but from the Imperial point of view they have drawn closer together distant portions of the Empire with the Motherland. With our leased wire between the Pacific ocean and Montreal, it seems to me that we could easily cover the last gap between Montreal and the Atlantic coast by using the Government line along the St. Lawrence to Labrador. It would not cost $2,500,000 to lay an Atlantic cable, including the stations and the repair vessel. At the conference of 1911, when the wireless systems were as well known as they are to-day, the conference, led by Mr. Asquith, Sir Wilfrid. Laurier, Sir Joseph Ward and other Imperial statesmen, expressed the opinion that it was not the wireless system, but a cable which was needed in order to give the British Empire cheap telegraphic communication. The resolution passed by the conference was to the effect that if the cable companies did not materially reduce their rates, the Imperial Conference was of the opinion that the time would soon come when an Atlantic cable should be laid on the same principle as the Pacific cable. It is true the cable companies have somewhat reduced their rates, but I agree with my hon. friend that the reduction is only infinitesimal. We are told that a cheaper rate will be given under this legislation and that a guarantee deposit will be made by the Poulsen Company, but the more I read the Bill and the agreement, the less I see the permanency of that deposit. They deposit the money, it is true, but it will soon vanish, from what I gather in the contract. I have no objection to giving the Poulsen system a trial, but my hon. friend should not think that it is, as they say in Paris:	le dernier cri. I am afraid
we will have a conflict between the Marconi wireless and the Poulsen system. Although each company will guarantee that it will not be troubled by the waves of the other, yet in the wireless world there is continual interference. I would infer from the remarks made by the Postmaster General that the Poulsen concern is a British concern, but I am informed that it is an American corporation. This Bill contains the usual clauses. There is a contradiction between clause 3, which creates the Government Ocean Telegraph Board, and clause 9, which gives certain powers to the Eailway Commission. It seems to me that the members of the Cabinet have already so many duties to perform that they should not take upon themselves the administration of a department which is so very technical in its nature, but that they should rather leave to the Railway Board to deal with the wireless. I think the Railway Board has the necessary powers, not only to deal with railways, but with cables and telegraphs, and I* think wireless.
Not cables.

the legislation.
It was conditional.

Yes. One of the other important parts of the Bill is that it does not refer only to the wireless system, but the board we are creating is to have control of the business of the cable companies so far as Canada is concerned. As a matter of fact, we do not need the board so much for the wireless as for the cable business. Having the responsibility of this matter, desirous as I am of breaking the prices which Canadians have had to pay in the past to the cable companies, I do not see my way clear to disagree with Mr. Samuel, the British Postmaster General, when he tells me, with his wide experience and with the first-class officers he has in his department, that this is not the time to lay a state-owned cable. For they see

far ahead of them, and they believe that the wireless, as my hon. friend has put it has not said its last word. the wireless seems to be advancing by leaps and bounds, and in the near future it may be not merely as efficient as the cable, but more efficient; instead of the present rate of forty words a minute, this company guarantees double that amount, and if they do not carry out their guarantee, they lose all their privileges. The more stringent we made the regulations, the more emphatically they said: Our system is so good that you can place upon our operations all the restrictions you like. If this succeeds, my hon. friend will not ask us to invest a large sum of money in a cable, the usefulness of which may be equalled or surpassed by this wireless system. The British Government has sufficient faith in this company to grant them a license, and they say that the moment everything is _ in _ shape they are ready to give us a service in a few months. We are not bound to these people either financially or morally. So far as ocean business is concerned, the Marconi has not been a success. I do not want to cnti-cise the Marconi system, but for some reason they have not been recognized or looked upon as successful competitors of the cable companies. I am bound to say that they are improving their system, and suppose that in the near future, instead of having the cables alone, we shall have the Marconi, the Poulsen, and the cable, and this country will then be free from the very heavy charges to which we have been subjected. If not, I shall have to come to this House before long, because the experiment will be short, and ask for authority to expend the necessary money for the establishment of a through telegraphic connection between Canada and the British Empire.

I wish to congratulate the Postmaster General on the great amount of effort he has put forth in bringing this measure before the House, and I sincerely hope that he will bring about all that he anticipates with regard to the transmission of messages across the Atlantic. I desire again to put myself on record as being strongly in favour-more strongly than I have time to express myself tb-night-of the appointment of a commission to look into the matter of wireless telegraphy, with a view to deciding on the system which we could best make use of in this country. I am satisfied that there will be a great duel of coniiiction of interests between the Marconi system and this system if they both operate. I do not wish to take up the time of the House tonight discussing this matter at length; I merely wish to place myself on record as being strongly in favour of a state-owned Mr. PELLETIER.

In case the Government contemplate bringing down further supplementary estimates, I have received from Montreal a letter from an old soldier in which he states that the two old military cemeteries at Montreal are being desecrated by boys. The lettering on the tombs has disappeared, the walls and fences are in very poor condition. This old soldier says that we owe to the pioneers of the British system in Canada, the sacred duty of protecting their ashes. It would be a matter of a few hundred dollars, possibly a thousand dollars, to put the two cemeteries in decent condition. I would ask my hon. friend to attend to this at once. This old soldier appeals to me and I am very glad indeed to re-echo his appeal to the House of Commons, and I would like my hon. friend to attend to this before Parliament prorogues. It will really be to the credit of the country to protect the ashes of these old soldiers.
